text: Abnormal Psychology, Cheatsheet MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-05 · The abnormal patch. How to use. Goes deeper than the high-yield revision sheet. Read once for coverage, then revise off tables + red TRAP boxes. Anything you blank on, mark it and re-read the matching section on the next pass. 1. Defining Abnormality (4 Ds) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation. Distress — subjective suffering. Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning. Danger — risk to self or others. TRAP: Deviance alone ≠ abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. Always need at least distress or dysfunction with it. Some textbooks list a 5th D: Duration , especially for chronicity criteria (≥ 6 months, ≥ 2 years, etc.). 2. Historical Models Era Model Key name(s) Prehistoric Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek / Roman Biological, four humors Hippocrates, Galen Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum (1487) Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (Bicêtre, "moral treatment"), Tuke (York Retreat) 19th c. Biological, classification Kraepelin ( dementia praecox ), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia , 4 As) Early 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism) Mid 20th c. Cognitive-behavioral Beck (depression), Ellis (REBT) 1980s+ Biopsychosocial integration Engel (1977) TRAP: Kraepelin coined dementia praecox . Bleuler renamed it schizophrenia ("split mind", referring to fragmented thought, not split personality). Don't confuse with DID. 3. Approaches to Psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT, psychosurgery Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association, transference Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Beck), REBT (Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Rogers), Gestalt (Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma, oppression Family therapy, community psychology Biopsychosocial All three interact ( Engel, 1977 ) Integrative Diathesis-stress Predisposition × stressor Reduce both load 4. DSM-5 vs ICD-11 DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019) Publisher APA , US-centric WHO , global Use Clinical + research Clinical + epidemiology + billing Sections 3 sections, 22 chapters; no axes (dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental, behavioral, neurodevelopmental OCD Own chapter (separated from anxiety) Own chapter PTSD Own chapter (Trauma- and stressor-related) Own chapter, also adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed (no more paranoid/catatonic/etc.) Removed "Mental Retardation" Renamed Intellectual Developmental Disorder Disorders of Intellectual Development Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed (you can dx MDD within 2 mo of loss) More cautious approach Hoarding, Excoriation New in DSM-5 Also recognized Gender dysphoria Renamed from "Gender Identity Disorder" Moved out of mental disorders chapter to "Conditions related to sexual health" TRAP: Multi-axial system was DSM-IV . DSM-5 dropped axes. If a question references "Axis I disorder" it's testing pre-DSM-5 vocabulary. 5. Mental Status Exam (MSE), order matters ABS-MTPCIJ : A ppearance, B ehavior, S peech, M ood/affect, T hought (form + content), P erception, C ognition, I nsight, J udgment. Mood = subjective ("how do you feel?"). Affect = observed (range, congruence, intensity). Thought form = how thoughts flow (loose, tangential, flight of ideas, circumstantial, blocking, perseveration). Thought content = what (delusions, suicidal/homicidal ideation, obsessions, phobias). Perception = hallucinations (auditory, visual, etc.), illusions, depersonalization. Cognition = orientation, attention, memory, abstract thinking. Insight = awareness of being ill. Judgment = decision-making in real situations. 6. Anxiety Disorders Disorder Core feature Duration Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + worry about more / behavior change Attack peaks ≤ 10 min Specific Phobia Marked fear of single object/situation ≥ 6 months Social Anxiety Disorder Fear of scrutiny, judgment in social situations ≥ 6 months Agoraphobia Fear of places where escape/help is hard (≥ 2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Disorder Excessive fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wk (kids), ≥ 6 mo (adults) Selective Mutism Failure to speak in specific social situations despite ability ≥ 1 month (not first month of school) TRAP: OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5 (its own chapter, see §7). Same for PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related chapter, see §8). 7. OCD & Related Disorders OCD — obsessions (intrusive thoughts) + compulsions (repetitive acts to neutralize). Ego-dystonic. Time-consuming (≥ 1 hr/day) or distressing. Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) — preoccupation with perceived flaw in appearance. Hoarding Disorder — persistent difficulty discarding possessions. New in DSM-5 . Trichotillomania — recurrent hair-pulling. Excoriation — recurrent skin-picking. New in DSM-5 . TRAP: OCPD ≠ OCD . OCPD = perfectionist, rigid personality style , ego-syntonic, in the personality disorders chapter. OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions, in OCD-related chapter. 8. Trauma- & Stressor-Related PTSD — exposure to actual/threatened death/serious injury/sexual violence + intrusion symptoms (flashbacks, nightmares) + avoidance + negative alterations in cognition/mood + arousal/reactivity. Duration > 1 month . Acute Stress Disorder — same symptom clusters but duration 3 days to 1 month . Adjustment Disorders — emotional/behavioral symptoms within 3 months of stressor; doesn't meet criteria for another disorder. Block 2, key disorders deep-dive 75 min Six disorder clusters that show up on every paper. Read each, drill the trap, write the duration / criteria threshold from memory before moving on. 2.1 Mood (cheatsheet §9), 12 min MDD : SIG-E-CAPS, ≥ 5 of 9, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia, ≥ 2 wks. Persistent Depressive (Dysthymia) : ≥ 2 yrs (≥ 1 yr in kids). Bipolar I : ≥ 1 manic episode (≥ 1 wk, or any duration if hospitalised). MDE not required. Bipolar II : hypomania (≥ 4 days) + MDE. Never full mania. Cyclothymia : hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode, ≥ 2 yrs. DIG-FAST for mania: Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity, Sleep ↓, Talkativeness. TRAP: One full manic episode in their entire history → Bipolar I, even if all current episodes are hypomanic. 2.2 Psychosis (cheatsheet §10), 15 min Schizophrenia : ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative sx). title: Action Potential — Complete MET Reference
text: Action Potential — Complete MET Reference The single most testable neurophysiology topic across MET, NIMHANS, AIIMS. Built around ion movement (Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cl-), the four phases, and the rules that make MCQs predictable. 0. What an Action Potential Actually Is (start here) An action potential is the basic signal a neuron uses to talk. It is a short (~1 millisecond) electrical pulse that travels down the axon from the cell body to the axon terminal. When it reaches the terminal, it causes neurotransmitter release, which then signals the next neuron. Every thought, sensation, movement, and emotion you have is built out of millions of these pulses firing in patterns. So the question “how does a neuron fire?” = “how does an action potential happen?” The one-sentence story When a neuron is at rest, the inside of its membrane is negative relative to the outside (about -70 millivolts). When the neuron is stimulated enough, ion channels open in a precise sequence — first sodium (Na+) rushes IN making the inside briefly positive , then potassium (K+) rushes OUT bringing it back to negative — and that pulse of voltage change propagates down the axon at up to 120 m/s. That’s it. Everything else in this primer is the mechanics of how that pulse is generated, shaped, and propagated. Five things you must know before the mechanics make sense Neurons have a charged membrane at rest. Inside is at -70 mV, outside is the reference (0 mV). This charge difference is called the resting membrane potential (RMP) . It exists because the membrane lets some ions cross more easily than others (mostly K+ leaks out a little, leaving the inside negative). The membrane is studded with ion channels. Some are always open (“leak channels”), some open only when voltage changes (“voltage-gated”), some open only when a chemical binds (“ligand-gated”). The action potential is driven by voltage-gated channels for Na+ and K+. Ions flow because of two forces: concentration and charge. Na+ wants to enter (lots outside, little inside, attracted to negative interior). K+ wants to leave (lots inside, little outside, but pulled back by negative interior). When a channel opens, the relevant ion moves whichever way its forces dictate. Knowing which ion goes which way at each phase is the whole game. An action potential is “all or none.” If the stimulus is strong enough to push the membrane to about -55 mV (the threshold ), a full action potential fires. If the stimulus is weaker, nothing happens. Bigger stimuli do not produce bigger APs — they produce more APs per second (frequency coding). One AP looks identical to every other AP in that neuron. The signal travels because each segment of axon triggers the next segment. Na+ entering at one spot depolarizes the next bit of membrane to threshold, which opens its Na+ channels, and so on. In myelinated axons, the AP “skips” between exposed gaps (Nodes of Ranvier), which is way faster than continuous conduction. What an action potential looks like on a graph Voltage on Y-axis (in mV), time on X-axis (in milliseconds). The whole thing takes about 2 ms. +30 ─────────────●─── PEAK (Na+ channels inactivate) ╱│╲ ╱ │ ╲ ╱ │ ╲ ← REPOLARIZATION (K+ flowing OUT) ╱ │ ╲ ╱ │ ╲ -55 ────●─╱─────│─────●──── THRESHOLD (-55 mV) ╱ │ ╲ ╱ ↑ │ ╲___ -70 ─● DEPOL │ \____ ← AFTERHYPERPOLARIZATION | (Na+ IN)│ (K+ channels still open RMP briefly, overshoots RMP) Why exams hammer this topic Action potential MCQs test precise, factual recall of: - Which ion moves at which phase (Na+ in for depolarization, K+ out for repolarization, Ca2+ in at the terminal for NT release, Cl- in for IPSP) - Which channels open and when (voltage-gated Na+ at threshold, voltage-gated K+ slightly later, voltage-gated Ca2+ at the axon terminal) - Refractory periods (absolute = Na+ inactivated, relative = K+ still open) - Conduction speed and myelin (saltatory in myelinated fibers, fastest in A-alpha) - Synaptic transmission cascade (AP arrives → Ca2+ in → vesicles fuse → NT released → binds postsynaptic receptors → EPSP or IPSP) If you know the story below cold, you will get every single one right. If you confuse Na+ and K+, mix up depolarization and repolarization, or don’t know that Ca2+ triggers NT release, you will bleed marks. The 6 questions you got wrong on the diagnostic were all in this cluster. Now that the big picture is set, here is the mechanics in detail. 1. Resting Membrane Potential (RMP) The neuron at rest sits at about -70 mV (range -60 to -90 depending on neuron type). Inside is negative relative to outside. Why -70 mV? Three forces. Force What it does Effect Concentration gradient K+ wants to leave (high inside), Na+ wants to enter (high outside) Sets up the chemistry Electrical gradient Inside is negative, attracts cations Opposes K+ leaving Selective permeability at rest Membrane is ~50x more permeable to K+ than Na+ (leak channels) K+ dominates The membrane settles where K+ efflux balances the electrical pull keeping K+ in. That equilibrium = ~-70 mV (close to K+’s equilibrium potential of -90 mV, dragged up by small Na+ leak). Ion concentrations (mEq/L), memorize this table Ion Inside Outside Equilibrium potential (Eion) K+ 140 (high) 5 (low) -90 mV Na+ 15 (low) 145 (high) +60 mV Cl- 10 (low) 110 (high) -65 mV Ca2+ 0.0001 (very low) 2 (high) +120 mV Memory hook: “K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out.” Na+/K+ pump (Na+/K+ ATPase) Pumps 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in , using 1 ATP. Electrogenic : net export of +1 charge per cycle, contributes ~-4 mV to RMP. Maintains the gradients but does NOT directly cause RMP. RMP is caused by K+ leak channels following the K+ gradient. The pump just keeps the gradient charged up. Common MCQ trap: “What sets resting potential?” Answer: K+ permeability via leak channels. NOT the Na+/K+ pump (it’s the gradient-maintainer, not the voltage-setter). 2. title: Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer
text: Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer Psychological Assessment, Read-First Primer This is written in explanation mode. Read it like a chapter, not a cheatsheet. Every fact has a “why” attached. Once this clicks, the 60-question Bio + Testing drill stops being a confusion machine and starts being a self-test. If you walk away with one mental model, it is this: a psychological test is a measuring instrument, and like any instrument, it has to be (a) consistent and (b) accurate. Consistent = reliability. Accurate = validity. Everything else in this section is either a way to estimate reliability, a way to estimate validity, a way to interpret scores against norms, or an example of a real-world test. That is the whole map. 1. Why test construction is even a thing Psychology is uncomfortably stuck between two facts. First, the things we want to measure (anxiety, intelligence, personality) are not directly observable. There is no anxiety-meter you can clip to a fingertip. Second, we still need to make decisions: should this child be in special education? Is this candidate fit for the army? Does this patient have OCD? So we build instruments out of items, like a thermometer made of questions. That is why item analysis exists. Each item is a single sensor reading. If the sensor is too easy (everyone gets it right) it tells us nothing. If the sensor is too hard (no one gets it) it tells us nothing. If the sensor agrees with the rest of the test, it is doing its job. If it disagrees, something is wrong with that item. Difficulty index, p The difficulty index is just the proportion who got an item right. p = (number who got the item right) / (total who attempted) Range zero to one. p = 0.50 means half the test-takers got it right. That is the sweet spot for a free-response item, because it discriminates the most. For a 4-option MCQ, the sweet spot is closer to 0.625 because guessers will pick the right answer 25% of the time by chance, and you want item difficulty to land halfway between guessing (0.25) and ceiling (1.00). Items with p above 0.80 are too easy and items below 0.20 are too hard. Both are candidates for revision because they cannot tell strong students from weak ones. Discrimination index, D This one asks: do the test-takers who scored well on the whole test do better on this item than the test-takers who scored badly? Specifically: D = p_upper - p_lower Where p_upper is the proportion correct in the top 27% of scorers and p_lower is the proportion in the bottom 27%. Range is minus one to plus one. If D is high (above 0.40), the item agrees with the overall test. Top scorers got it right, bottom scorers got it wrong. The item is a good signal. If D is near zero, the item is random noise. Both groups perform similarly. If D is negative , something is wrong. The bottom group out-performed the top group. That happens when an item is mis-keyed, ambiguously worded, or has a trick that strong test-takers over-think. Negative D means discard immediately. Always read negative D as a red flag, not as a hard item. 2. Reliability, the consistency story Reliability is not about whether the test is correct. It is about whether the test is consistent . A bathroom scale that reads 75 kg every time you step on it is reliable, even if it is calibrated wrong and the true weight is 70. A scale that bounces between 60, 90, and 80 is unreliable, full stop. Why does this matter? Because if a test is unreliable, you cannot trust any single score from it. The next time you give the same test to the same person, you will get a different answer for reasons that have nothing to do with the trait you are trying to measure. You are measuring noise. The classical test theory equation summarizes this: Observed Score = True Score + Error Reliability is the proportion of observed score variance that is true variance, not error. A reliability of 0.80 says 80% of what you are seeing is signal, 20% is noise. There are several reliability methods because there are several ways to think about “consistency”: Across time: test the same person twice on different days (test-retest). Across forms: give two different versions of the test (parallel forms). Within one administration, across items: check that the items hang together (split-half, Cronbach alpha, KR-20). Across raters: check that two judges agree (Cohen kappa for categorical, ICC for continuous). Test-retest, the time-stability check Give the test on Monday, give it again three weeks later, correlate the two scores. If the correlation is high, the test is stable across time. The trap: if you wait too long, the trait itself can change, and the correlation drops not because the test is bad but because the person actually changed. If you wait too short, memory carryover inflates the correlation. The standard window is two to four weeks. Split-half plus Spearman-Brown Give the test once, split the items into two halves (often odd-numbered vs even-numbered), and correlate the two halves. The result tells you how internally consistent the test is. Catch: by splitting, you have effectively halved the test length, and shorter tests are less reliable. So the raw split-half correlation underestimates the full-test reliability. Spearman-Brown corrects for that: r_full = 2 * r_half / (1 + r_half) If r_half is 0.60, the full-test estimated reliability is 1.20 / 1.60 = 0.75. Spearman-Brown is the standard fix you apply after any split. Cronbach alpha Imagine doing every possible split-half (odd-even, first-half last-half, items 1-3-5 vs 2-4-6, etc.) and averaging the result. That mean is Cronbach alpha. It is the most common internal-consistency measure for tests with multi-point items (like Likert). Important: alpha is not a measure of unidimensionality. A test can have high alpha and still be measuring two distinct constructs. Alpha rises with item count, item homogeneity, and variance in the trait. The MET love this trap. text: Biopsychology — Carlson depth pass Source: Carlson & Birkett, Physiology of Behavior (the book Sihan named on 2026-05-28). This page is the delta on top of the Pinel chapter : it walks the systems Carlson goes deeper on than Pinel does, in Carlson's order, and locks the parts NIMHANS / MET love to test. Built 2026-05-28 — first section of the per-section depth pass rollout. Use this after reading the Pinel chapter ; together they cover the section in full. Why a Carlson pass on top of Pinel? The two books overlap on the basics (neurons, anatomy, vision/audition, sensorimotor, plasticity, lateralisation) but diverge on the mechanism-heavy systems. Carlson goes much deeper on (1) the mesolimbic reward circuit and drug-of-abuse mechanisms , (2) sleep neurochemistry and the flip-flop switch , (3) hunger as an arcuate-nucleus loop , (4) HPA axis + glucocorticoid feedback + hippocampal atrophy , (5) organising vs activating effects of gonadal hormones , (6) the molecular cascade for LTP , and (7) neurobiology of the major psychiatric disorders as a single mechanism-first chapter. That is what is unpacked below. Anything Pinel already nails (cranial nerves, visual receptive fields, split brain, Korsakoff) is not repeated here — read those on the Pinel page. Jump to: 1. How Carlson is organised 2. Neurotransmitter systems, by system 3. Reward circuit & mesolimbic DA 4. Drugs of abuse — mechanism by class 5. Sleep neurochemistry & the flip-flop switch 6. Hunger — arcuate POMC/AgRP loop 7. HPA axis, glucocorticoids & the hippocampus 8. Sex hormones — organising vs activating 9. LTP — the molecular cascade 10. Neurobiology of the major disorders 11. Sensorimotor — what Carlson adds 12. Emotion — amygdala in detail 13. NIMHANS-tilt: clinical hooks 14. Carlson vs Pinel — every divergence 15. MCQ traps Carlson sets that Pinel does not 16. Self-test 1. How Carlson is organised (and why that matters) Carlson is a mechanism-first physiology book , not a "tour of the field" book. Pinel writes around case studies and divisions ; Carlson writes around systems : neurotransmitter system → behavior it produces → drug that hits that system → disorder when it fails. If a question asks "which transmitter / which circuit / which receptor / which drug", Carlson is the book it was written from. His chapters (in his order, condensed): structure of the nervous system → neurons & conduction → synaptic transmission → drugs & receptors → methods → vision → audition & somatosenses → control of movement → sleep → reproductive behavior → emotion → ingestive behavior → learning & memory → communication → neurological disorders → schizophrenia, mood disorders, anxiety → autism, ADHD, stress, addiction. Lock it: when an MCQ stem names a receptor subtype (D2, 5-HT2A, NMDA, GABA-A α1, μ-opioid), a circuit (mesolimbic, nigrostriatal, mesocortical, tuberoinfundibular, locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe), or a drug class with its mechanism (NSRI, MAO-B inhibitor, atypical antipsychotic), reach for Carlson, not Pinel. 2. Neurotransmitter systems, system by system Carlson's signature move: don't memorise transmitters in a list, learn each one as a system (cell-body cluster → projection pathway → receptors → behavior → drug). NIMHANS leans on these. Dopamine — three pathways, one transmitter Pathway From → To Function What happens when it fails Nigrostriatal Substantia nigra (pars compacta) → dorsal striatum (caudate + putamen) Motor initiation, habit learning Loss = Parkinson's disease Mesolimbic Ventral tegmental area (VTA) → nucleus accumbens (NAc, ventral striatum), amygdala, hippocampus Reward, motivation, "wanting" Hyperactivity = positive symptoms of schizophrenia; addiction hijacks it Mesocortical VTA → prefrontal cortex Working memory, executive control, motivation Hypoactivity = negative symptoms of schizophrenia Tuberoinfundibular Arcuate nucleus (hypothalamus) → median eminence Inhibits prolactin release D2-blocking antipsychotics → hyperprolactinaemia → amenorrhoea, gynaecomastia Receptors: 5 subtypes, two families. D1-like (D1, D5) are G s -coupled → ↑ cAMP. D2-like (D2, D3, D4) are G i -coupled → ↓ cAMP. Classical antipsychotics block D2 . Atypicals add 5-HT2A blockade. TRAP — DA pathway naming. "Mesolimbic" and "mesocortical" share the VTA origin; the difference is the target. Mesolimbic → NAc (reward) ; mesocortical → PFC (cognition) . "Nigrostriatal" is a separate origin (substantia nigra, not VTA). Norepinephrine — one nucleus, the whole brain Cell bodies live in the locus coeruleus (pons). One small cluster projects diffusely across cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebellum, spinal cord. Function: arousal, vigilance, attention to novelty . NE firing rises during alertness, falls during sleep, peaks during stress. α1, α2, β1, β2, β3 receptors. β-blockers cross the blood-brain barrier (propranolol) → reduce somatic anxiety. Serotonin (5-HT) — raphe nuclei, fourteen receptors Cell bodies: raphe nuclei (midline brainstem). Dorsal raphe → forebrain, midbrain ; median raphe → limbic system; caudal raphe → spinal cord. ≥14 receptor subtypes; the exam-relevant ones: 5-HT1A — autoreceptor on raphe neurons; postsynaptic in hippocampus. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist (anxiolytic). 5-HT2A — psychedelic site (LSD, psilocybin agonists); atypical antipsychotics antagonise it. 5-HT3 — the only ionotropic 5-HT receptor; ondansetron antagonist (antiemetic). Extended concept bank (per chapter) 23. Fast glossary (A–Z) 24. Self-test (by chapter) 1. Biopsychology as a neuroscience (Pinel ch. 1) The one idea behind the whole book. Biopsychology is the scientific study of the biology of behaviour : it asks how the nervous system produces what we think, feel and do. It is one branch of neuroscience (the larger study of the nervous system), the branch that keeps behaviour at the centre. Pinel's recurring lesson is that mind and brain are not two things: every thought is a physical event in tissue. The six divisions of biopsychology Pinel splits the field by what you study and how . Learn each by its defining method, because the paper tests "which division does X?". Division What it studies Typical method Physiological psychology Neural mechanisms of behaviour Direct manipulation of the brain in controlled experiments (lesions, stimulation), usually in lab animals Psychopharmacology Effects of drugs on behaviour and the brain Manipulate behaviour with drugs; develop therapeutic drugs Neuropsychology Psychological effects of brain damage in human patients Case studies + standardised tests; the most applied division (NIMHANS leans here) Psychophysiology Relation between physiology and behaviour using non-invasive body measures in healthy humans EEG, heart rate, skin conductance (GSR), pupil size Cognitive neuroscience Neural bases of cognition (thought, memory, attention) Mainly functional brain imaging (fMRI, PET) in humans Comparative psychology Behaviour across species, evolution, genetics, ethology Cross-species comparison, naturalistic + lab study TRAP — psychophysiology vs physiological psychology. Both have "physiolog" in the name. Physiological psychology = invasive manipulation of the brain, usually in animals . Psychophysiology = non-invasive recording from the surface of healthy humans . And neuropsychology = the study of human brain-damaged patients. Kinds of research, kinds of inference Pure vs applied. Pure = curiosity-driven knowledge; applied = solving a practical problem. Most real work is a blend. Experiments vs non-experiments. Only a true experiment (the researcher manipulates an independent variable and randomly assigns) can support a causal claim. Quasi-experiments and case studies cannot fully rule out confounds. Converging operations. Because every single method is flawed, biopsychology trusts a conclusion only when several different methods point the same way . This is Pinel's signature methodological value. The Morgan's Canon / law of parsimony spirit: prefer the simplest explanation that fits, and do not attribute a higher mental process when a lower one will do. Lock it: human brain-damaged patients = neuropsychology ; drugs = psychopharmacology ; non-invasive measures in healthy humans = psychophysiology ; imaging of cognition = cognitive neuroscience ; animal brain manipulation = physiological psychology ; across species = comparative . Recap §1. Biopsychology = biology of behaviour, six divisions sorted by method. Causation needs a true experiment. Converging operations: trust the conclusion many methods agree on. 2. Evolution, genetics & experience (Pinel ch. 2) The problem this chapter fixes. The old "nature versus nurture" question is a false dichotomy. Pinel's "nature-nurture done right" is that genes and experience are not rival causes adding up to 100%; they interact continuously. A trait is the product of a genetic program read out in an environment. You cannot say a behaviour is "60% genetic" for an individual, only how much variation in a population is associated with genetic variation (heritability). Evolution of the brain Natural selection (Darwin): heritable traits that improve fitnes

Descriptive Statistics Central tendency Mean — arithmetic average. Pulled by outliers. Median — middle value. Robust to outliers, best for skewed data. Mode — most frequent. Only measure for nominal data. Dispersion Range = max − min. IQR = Q3 − Q1. Used in box plots. Variance (σ²) = mean of squared deviations. Standard deviation (σ) = √variance. Same units as data. SEM = σ / √n. SD of the sampling distribution of the mean. Shape Skewness : positive (right tail; mean > median > mode), negative (left tail; mean < median < mode), zero (symmetric). Kurtosis : leptokurtic (peaked), mesokurtic (normal), platykurtic (flat). The normal distribution (mock-1 Q6) Symmetric, bell-shaped. Mean = median = mode. Empirical rule: ±1 SD covers ≈ 68% ; ±2 SD covers ≈ 95%; ±3 SD covers ≈ 99.7%. z-score = (X − μ) / σ. Standardises any score. T-score : M=50, SD=10. T=70 → +2 SD → 97.5th percentile (MMPI clinical cutoff). Stanine : M=5, SD=2, range 1–9. Sten : M=5.5, SD=2, range 1–10. 3. Probability + Sampling Sampling methods Method How Note Simple random Every unit equal probability Gold standard, requires sampling frame Systematic Every k-th unit from a list Risk if list has periodicity Stratified Divide into strata (e.g., gender), random sample within each Increases precision when strata differ on the variable Cluster Randomly select naturally occurring groups (schools, villages); often sample all units within (mock-1 Q5) Cheaper, less precise. Two-stage cluster samples within clusters. Multistage Combination of above National surveys Convenience Whoever is available Non-probability, biased Snowball Existing subjects recruit more Hidden populations, e.g. drug users Purposive / quota Investigator selects to fit categories Non-probability MCQ trap (mock-1 Q5): stratified divides population into strata then random samples within ; cluster randomly picks groups then samples all or many units per cluster. Both are probability methods. 4. Hypothesis Testing Setup H0 (null) = no effect / no difference / status quo. H1 (alternative) = effect exists. Two-tailed (any direction) vs one-tailed (specific direction). α = type I error rate (false positive). Conventionally 0.05. β = type II error rate (false negative). Power = 1 − β. Conventionally ≥ 0.80. Errors H0 true H0 false Reject H0 Type I (α, false +) Correct (power) Retain H0 Correct Type II (β, false −) Mock-1 Q1 trap: Type I = wrongly rejecting a TRUE null. (Wrongly retaining a false null = Type II.) p-value Probability of obtaining the observed result or more extreme if H0 were true. NOT the probability that H0 is true. If p < α → reject H0 (mock-1 Q3: p=0.03 < α=0.05 → reject). Statistically significant ≠ practically important. Always report effect size. Power Increases with: larger n, larger effect size, larger α, lower variability, one-tailed test. A priori power analysis sets sample size before data collection. Confidence intervals 95% CI: if we repeated the study many times, 95% of intervals would contain the true parameter. If 95% CI for a difference excludes 0 → significant at p < 0.05. 5. title: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory
text: Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems Theory Developmental Psychology · Exam-grade · Built 2026-05-05 1. Core Idea Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917-2005), Russian-born American developmental psychologist. Development is shaped by ongoing interaction between the person and a set of nested environmental systems . Originally Ecological Systems Theory , "The Ecology of Human Development" (1979). Later renamed Bioecological Model (1994, refined 2005) to give biology more weight and add the PPCT mechanism. Co-founded the Head Start program (1965) in the US, applied use of the theory. One-line answer: Development = person × proximal processes × nested context × time. 2. The 5 Systems (innermost to outermost) 2.1 Microsystem Immediate settings with direct face-to-face contact . Examples: family, school, peer group, neighbourhood, daycare, workplace (for adults). Influence is bidirectional : child shapes the environment, environment shapes the child. Most direct effect on development. 2.2 Mesosystem Interactions between two or more microsystems . Not a setting itself, a system of microsystems . Examples: parent-teacher communication, family-peer overlap, home-daycare links. Strong, supportive mesosystem links = better developmental outcomes. 2.3 Exosystem Settings the child does not directly participate in , but which still affect them via the microsystem. Examples: parent's workplace, school board decisions, mass media, parent's social network, local government policy. TRAP: Exosystem ≠ no influence. Child isn't in it, but it shapes them through their microsystem (e.g. dad loses job → stress at home → child's development affected). 2.4 Macrosystem The overarching cultural blueprint , the "cultural envelope" around all the other systems. Examples: ideologies, customs, laws, religion, SES, cultural values, economic system, war/peace. Doesn't refer to a specific setting, refers to the cultural patterning that shapes all settings. 2.5 Chronosystem The time dimension . Added later (after the original 4 systems). Three flavours of "time" effects: Life transitions , normative (school entry, puberty) and non-normative (parents' divorce, death of parent). Historical events the person lives through (pandemic, war, recession). Sociohistorical conditions of the cohort (cohort effects). TRAP: Chronosystem was added later . Older textbooks list only 4 systems. If a question says "Bronfenbrenner originally proposed 5 systems" — false. Originally 4, chronosystem added later. 3. Quick-Reference Table System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystems Parent-teacher meetings, home-school link Exosystem Indirect settings, child not in them Parent's workplace, school board, media Macrosystem Cultural blueprint Ideology, laws, religion, SES, customs Chronosystem Time dimension Divorce, pandemic, historical era 4. PPCT Model (1994 refinement, often asked) Bronfenbrenner refined the theory into the Bioecological Model using the PPCT mechanism. This is the engine of the modern version. 4.1 Process — proximal processes The engine of development . Most important driver. Regular, reciprocal interactions over extended time between the person and people/objects/symbols in the immediate environment. Examples: parent-child play, reading together, sustained peer activity, learning a skill from a mentor. Must be regular and over long stretches of time to count as proximal processes (not one-off events). 4.2 Person — individual traits Three sub-types: Sub-type Definition Examples Demand characteristics Visible traits that pull responses from others Age, gender, skin colour, physical appearance Resource characteristics Skills, abilities, experiences Intelligence, prior knowledge, social skills Force characteristics Temperament, motivation, persistence Curiosity, drive, distractibility, regulation 4.3 Context — the 5 nested systems Micro / Meso / Exo / Macro / Chrono. Already covered above. 4.4 Time Micro-time : continuity vs interruption within an activity (e.g. uninterrupted reading session). Meso-time : consistency of activities across days and weeks. Macro-time : chronosystem level, sociohistorical change across the lifespan. 5. High-Yield Exam Pointers Originally 4 systems , chronosystem added later. Bidirectionality is a key examiner trigger word, especially in microsystem questions. Theory has two phases: Ecological Systems Theory (1979) → Bioecological Model (1994) with PPCT. Proximal processes are the engine , not the context. Context modifies how proximal processes operate. Mesosystem is not a setting , it's a system of relationships between settings . 6. Compare and Contrast (very high-yield) Theorist Focus Mechanism Piaget Cognitive stages, internal Schemas, assimilation, accommodation Vygotsky Sociocultural ZPD, scaffolding (Bruner), more knowledgeable other Bronfenbrenner Ecological / multi-layered context Person × Process × Context × Time Erikson Psychosocial stages 8 crises across lifespan Bandura Social learning Observation, modeling, self-efficacy Rule of thumb: If the question stem mentions nested environments , cultural context , parent's workplace affecting child , or indirect influence → answer is Bronfenbrenner. 7. Applications Child welfare policy — interventions at multiple system levels (family + school + community). Inclusive education — coordinating microsystems (home, school, peers). Public health — tobacco control, vaccination uptake (macro + exo levels). Family therapy — recognising that family microsystem sits inside larger systems. Head Start program (Bronfenbrenner co-founded) — early childhood intervention targeting micro + meso systems. 8. Critique Hard to operationalise and test empirically — too many simultaneous variables. Originally underplayed biology (fixed in the bioecological revision via "Person" component). Criticised for being descriptive more than predictive , doesn't say which system dominates when.

Approaches to human cognition Eysenck & Keane open by saying cognitive psychology is not one method but four converging approaches , each with its own logic and limits. The point of knowing all four is that an exam stem will describe a technique and ask which approach it belongs to. Experimental cognitive psychology What it claims: you can infer the hidden stages of mental processing in healthy people by measuring behaviour under controlled conditions — chiefly reaction time (RT) and accuracy/error rate . It is the oldest strand and the historical core of the field. If a manipulation slows people down, that stage must require processing. Key logic: the subtraction/additive-factors idea — compare two tasks differing in one operation, and the RT difference estimates that operation's duration. Limit: behaviour alone is ambiguous about the underlying architecture (many models predict the same RT), and lab tasks may lack ecological validity. Cognitive neuropsychology + modularity What it claims: studying brain-damaged patients reveals the normal architecture of cognition, because damage can knock out one ability while sparing another. The bedrock assumption is modularity (Fodor): the mind contains specialised, domain-specific, informationally encapsulated modules that can be independently impaired. Key logic — the double dissociation : patient A is impaired on task X but fine on Y, while patient B is fine on X but impaired on Y. That pattern is strong evidence the two tasks rely on separate systems (one alone could be explained by task difficulty). Example: H.M. lost the ability to form new long-term memories yet had normal short-term span; other patients (e.g. K.F.) show the reverse — together a double dissociation of STM and LTM. Limit: damage is rarely clean, the brain reorganises, and single cases generalise poorly. Cognitive neuroscience methods What it claims: by measuring the living brain we can locate where and time when cognition happens. The methods trade off spatial against temporal resolution, and the exam loves to ask which method gives which. Method Measures Strength fMRI Blood-oxygen (BOLD) — indirect metabolic signal Excellent spatial resolution (mm), poor temporal (seconds); shows where . PET Radioactive tracer, blood flow/metabolism Good spatial, very poor temporal; needs injected tracer. EEG / ERP Scalp electrical activity; ERP = signal averaged to an event Excellent temporal resolution (ms), poor spatial; shows when . TMS Magnetic pulse that briefly disrupts a region Creates a "virtual lesion" → tests if a region is necessary (causal, not just correlational). Spatial vs temporal mnemonic: fMRI/PET = WHERE (great space, poor time). EEG/ERP = WHEN (great time, poor space). TMS = whether it's NECESSARY (causal). fMRI and EEG are merely correlational; only TMS and lesions establish that a region is causally required. Computational cognitive science & connectionism (PDP) What it claims: if a theory is precise enough, you can implement it as a running computer program; a model that actually reproduces human performance (including human errors ) is a strong test of the theory. The dominant style is connectionism / parallel distributed processing (PDP) : networks of simple, neuron-like units connected by weighted links, where knowledge is distributed across the pattern of weights rather than stored in one location, and learning happens by gradually adjusting weights (e.g. back-propagation). NIMHANS tests harder — connectionism. Be ready for the contrast with classical "symbolic" models. Symbolic (e.g. Newell & Simon's physical-symbol-system) manipulates discrete rules and symbols, processing serially. Connectionist/PDP uses distributed sub-symbolic representations and parallel processing; its hallmarks are graceful degradation (partial damage = partial loss, not total crash), generalisation, and learning from examples. NIMHANS may ask which framework explains prototype effects or developmental error patterns (e.g. the U-shaped curve in learning the past tense) — that's connectionism. Bottom-up vs top-down; serial vs parallel Two cross-cutting distinctions run through the whole book. Bottom-up (data-driven) processing starts from the stimulus and works up. Top-down (concept-driven) processing brings expectations, context and stored knowledge to bear. Theory, and the role of theory in counselling Sharf opens by asking what a theory of psychotherapy is and why a counsellor needs one. A theory is a coherent set of assumptions that explains how problems arise and how change happens; without one, a counsellor is improvising. A theory gives the clinician three things: a map of personality (what a person is made of and how distress develops), a set of goals , and a set of techniques that follow logically from the goals. A good theory , Sharf says, is precise / clear , comprehensive (covers a wide range of behaviour), parsimonious (no needless complexity), useful / applicable (generates testable predictions and practical methods), and verifiable / testable by research. He also sets up the recurring chapter frame used throughout the book: history of the originator , theory of personality , theory of psychotherapy (goals, the therapeutic relationship, assessment, techniques), application to a brief case , treatment of specific disorders, brief / short-term versions, current trends , use with diverse populations and gender issues , group counselling applications, a summary , and research / critique . Brief history. Counselling grew from several roots: Freud's psychoanalysis (the depth tradition), the vocational-guidance movement (Frank Parsons, early 1900s), psychometrics and the testing movement, and later the humanistic reaction (Rogers) and the behavioural / cognitive revolutions. The book then groups the theories into broad families: psychodynamic (Freud, Jung, Adler), humanistic / experiential (existential, person-centred, Gestalt), action / cognitive-behavioural (behaviour therapy, REBT, cognitive therapy, reality therapy), constructivist / postmodern (solution-focused, narrative), feminist , and family systems . Recap Ch 1. A theory = assumptions about personality + goals + techniques. A good theory is clear, comprehensive, parsimonious, useful, and testable. Every chapter follows the same frame: originator → personality → goals → relationship → techniques → applications → critique. Part Two · The psychodynamic approaches Ch 2. Psychoanalysis — Sigmund Freud Originator. Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), Viennese neurologist, founder of psychoanalysis. Working with hysteria (and Breuer's patient Anna O., source of the "talking cure"), he concluded symptoms have hidden mental causes in the unconscious. The first systematic theory of psychotherapy; the tradition every later theory reacts to. Theory of personality / how problems develop. Behaviour is driven by instincts (life/Eros with its energy libido , and death/Thanatos), and by an unconscious we cannot access directly. The mind has a topographic layout (conscious / preconscious / unconscious) and a structural one: the id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle, mediator), and superego (internalised morality). Personality forms through five psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital); over- or under-gratification produces fixation . Problems arise from unconscious conflict and unresolved early-childhood experience; the ego manages anxiety with defence mechanisms (repression the master defence, plus projection, displacement, reaction formation, sublimation, denial, regression, rationalisation, etc., catalogued by Anna Freud). text: Cranial Nerves I–XII What this is. The full I–XII table (name, type, function, common deficits) plus both mnemonics and the MCQ traps that hit every MET/NIMHANS paper. Spun out of the biopsych brain-anatomy note because you flagged it in Mock 1 and it deserves its own page. If you only memorise one biopsych side-page, make it this one. Full I–XII table Mnemonics Sensory vs motor vs both Parasympathetic carriers Brainstem nuclei map High-yield deficits MCQ traps Bedside testing Full I–XII table # Name Type Function Common deficit / MCQ hook I Olfactory Sensory Smell Only nerve that bypasses thalamus. Anosmia is first lost in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. Trauma to cribriform plate shears it off. II Optic Sensory Vision CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve (myelinated by oligodendrocytes, surrounded by meninges). Lesion at optic chiasm = bitemporal hemianopia (pituitary adenoma). III Oculomotor Motor (+parasym) Most extraocular muscles (SR, IR, MR, IO) + levator palpebrae + parasympathetic pupil constriction (Edinger-Westphal nucleus) + lens accommodation. Full palsy = ptosis + "down & out" eye + fixed dilated pupil. Uncal herniation compresses III early (blown pupil). IV Trochlear Motor Superior oblique (depresses + intorts adducted eye). Smallest CN. Only CN that decussates before exit AND only one to exit dorsally from brainstem. Vertical diplopia worse going down stairs; patient tilts head away from lesion. V Trigeminal Both Sensation of face (V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular) + cornea + ant ⅔ scalp + dura. Motor: muscles of mastication. Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) — V2/V3 most common. Corneal reflex afferent. Jaw deviates toward weak side on opening. VI Abducens Motor Lateral rectus (abduction). Longest intracranial course → first CN affected by raised ICP. False localising sign. Lesion = inability to abduct, horizontal diplopia on lateral gaze to lesion side. VII Facial Both (+parasym) Muscles of facial expression + stapedius + posterior belly digastric. Taste anterior ⅔ tongue (chorda tympani). Parasympathetic: lacrimal + submandibular + sublingual glands. Bell's palsy (LMN, idiopathic) = whole half-face including forehead. UMN lesion (stroke) spares forehead (bilateral cortical innervation upper face). Hyperacusis if stapedius involved. VIII Vestibulocochlear Sensory Cochlear: hearing. Vestibular: balance + head position. Acoustic neuroma = vestibular schwannoma at cerebellopontine angle (CPA) → unilateral sensorineural hearing loss + tinnitus + vertigo, later facial/trigeminal signs. Bilateral acoustic neuromas = NF2. IX Glossopharyngeal Both (+parasym) Sensation posterior ⅓ tongue + pharynx + middle ear + carotid sinus. Motor: stylopharyngeus. Taste posterior ⅓ tongue. Parasympathetic: parotid gland. Gag reflex AFFERENT limb (efferent is X). Glossopharyngeal neuralgia triggered by swallowing. X Vagus Both (+parasym) Motor: palate (except tensor veli palatini = V3), pharynx, larynx (via recurrent laryngeal). Sensation: larynx, pharynx, viscera. Parasympathetic: thoracic + abdominal viscera down to splenic flexure. Taste: epiglottis. Gag reflex EFFERENT limb. Uvula deviates AWAY from lesion. Recurrent laryngeal palsy → hoarse voice (left longer course, loops under aortic arch = vulnerable). Vagal stimulation ↓HR. title: Degrees of Freedom — finally understand it
text: Degrees of Freedom — finally understand it The one statistics idea everyone memorises as " n − 1 " and almost nobody actually gets . This page builds it from zero with one idea you carry the whole way through, so by the end you can look at any test and say why its df is what it is, instead of recalling a formula. No prior stats needed. Read it top to bottom once and it sticks. 1 The one idea 2 Simplest example 3 A df is a constraint 4 Why variance uses n−1 5 df in every test 6 df changes the curve MCQ traps Self-test 1. The one idea Degrees of freedom = how many numbers are still free to be anything, once you have already fixed some fact about them. Every fact you fix (a total, a mean, an estimate) locks one number down, so that number is no longer free. Count the values, subtract the facts you have pinned. That's it. Everything below is just this sentence applied. The phrase sounds technical but the idea is everyday. "Freedom" here means freedom to vary — to take any value. A degree of freedom is one independent number that you could still change without breaking a rule you have agreed to. The moment a rule forces a number to be one specific value, it has lost its freedom and stops counting. Why the name. It comes from physics: a particle moving in 3D space has 3 degrees of freedom (it can move along x, y, z). Pin it to a tabletop and it has 2. Pin it to a wire and it has 1. Each constraint removes one direction it's free to move. Statistics borrows the word exactly: each thing you fix about your data removes one direction the data is free to move. 2. The simplest possible example Forget statistics for a second. I tell you: "I'm thinking of three numbers, and they add up to 10 ." How many of those numbers can you freely guess? You can pick the first one. Say 4 . Still free. You can pick the second one. Say 3 . Still free. Now the third number is not a guess any more — it has to be 3 , because the three must sum to 10 (4 + 3 + 3 = 10). The total forced the last number. Three numbers, one rule (the total), so 2 are free and 1 is forced . Degrees of freedom = 3 − 1 = 2 . The "−1" is the one fact you fixed: the sum. This is the whole mechanism. If I'd said "I'm thinking of n numbers with a fixed total," then n − 1 of them are free and the last is always determined. df = n − 1. Not because of a magic rule, but because fixing the total uses up exactly one number's freedom. Carry this picture: the last value is the "dependent" one — it has to mop up whatever's needed to satisfy the rule. The number of free choices before you hit the forced one is the degrees of freedom. 3. A degree of freedom is spent by every quantity you estimate In real statistics the "rule you fixed" is almost always this: you calculated a statistic from the data and then reused it. The most common one is the sample mean . Here's the link. To work out how spread out a sample is, you first need its mean. But the mean is computed from the same data . Once you know the mean of n scores, the scores are no longer all free — they must be consistent with that mean. Just like the total in the example, the mean is a fixed fact, so it forces the last score. Worked feel for it. Five exam scores have a mean of 70, so they must sum to 350. You're free to set the first four: 60, 80, 75, 65 (they sum to 280). The fifth is no longer yours to choose — it must be 70 to make the total 350. Four free, one forced. df = 5 − 1 = 4. General rule: df = (number of observations) − (number of parameters you estimated from those observations). Each parameter you estimate from the data costs one degree of freedom, because using it imposes one constraint. Estimate one quantity (the mean) → lose 1 df. Estimate two quantities (e.g. a slope and an intercept in regression) → lose 2 df. This single principle predicts the df for every test, which is why it's worth owning instead of memorising each formula. They swap these: df is not "the sample size." It's the sample size minus the estimates you've made. A question that says "with n = 20, the t-test df is 20" is wrong: a one-sample t uses the mean, so df = 19. 4. Why sample variance divides by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) This is the classic exam point, and now you can actually reason it out instead of reciting it. Variance is the average squared distance of each score from the mean. For a whole population you divide by N, because you know the true mean and every score really is free: σ² = Σ(x − μ)² / N But with a sample you don't know the true population mean μ. You substitute the sample mean x̄, which you computed from the very same data. And the sample mean sits, by construction, right in the middle of your sample — it hugs your data more tightly than the unknown true mean would. So the deviations from x̄ are, on average, a little too small . Divide by n and you systematically underestimate the real spread. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n makes the estimate a touch larger, exactly correcting that bias. And n − 1 is precisely the degrees of freedom: you spent one on estimating the mean. s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1) You divide by n − 1 not as a fudge but because only n − 1 of the deviations are free. Once x̄ is fixed, the deviations (x − x̄) must sum to zero, so the last deviation is forced by the other n − 1. There are only n − 1 independent pieces of spread information, so you average over n − 1. NIMHANS depth: this is called Bessel's correction . The estimator s² with n − 1 is unbiased for σ² (its long-run average equals the true variance); dividing by n gives a biased (too small) estimator. Note a subtlety they sometimes probe: s (the SD, the square root) is still slightly biased even after the correction, but s² is unbiased. The correction targets the variance. Recap so far. df = values − things estimated from those values. Fix a total or a mean and the last value is forced. Sample variance divides by n − 1 because estimating the mean costs one df, leaving n − 1 independent deviations. 5. Degrees of freedom

title: Developmental Psychology, Cheatsheet
text: Developmental Psychology, Cheatsheet MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-05 · Patches the thin section, absorbs Bronfenbrenner write-up. How to use. This is the section-3 fleshing of dev psych. Read top-to-bottom once, then revise off the tables and the red TRAP boxes. Bronfenbrenner gets its own section here (5) since exam loves him; full primer at notes/bronfenbrenner if you want deeper. 1. Foundational Principles Principle Meaning Example Cephalocaudal Head → toe Head control before walking Proximodistal Center → periphery Trunk control before fine finger Continuity vs Discontinuity Gradual growth vs stage jumps Vocab growth (continuous) vs Piaget stages (discontinuous) Nature vs Nurture Genes vs environment, modern view = interactionist Twin studies, behavioral genetics Critical period Rigid window, miss it and the capacity is lost Lorenz imprinting in geese Sensitive period Flexible window, learning easier but still possible later L1 acquisition, depth perception Stability vs Change Do traits persist or shift across life? Temperament (mostly stable), IQ (some plasticity) Active vs Passive child Does the child shape their own development? Bidirectionality (Bronfenbrenner, Bell) TRAP: Critical = rigid biological window (lost if missed). Sensitive = optimal but flexible. Lorenz's imprinting = critical. Language learning = sensitive (you can still learn L2 at 30, just harder). 2. Prenatal Development & Teratogens Three prenatal stages Stage Duration Key event Germinal 0-2 weeks Zygote → blastocyst → implantation Embryonic 2-8 weeks Organogenesis, most vulnerable to teratogens Fetal 8 weeks-birth Growth + refinement, viability ~24 weeks Teratogens (high-yield) Alcohol — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD); FAS = facial anomalies, growth restriction, CNS damage. Most common preventable cause of intellectual disability. Tobacco — low birth weight, prematurity. Thalidomide — limb malformations (1950s-60s, classic teratogen exam case). Rubella — heart, eye, ear defects in 1st trimester. Lead, mercury — CNS damage. Zika — microcephaly. TRAP: Embryonic period (weeks 2-8) is most vulnerable, not the fetal period. Organs are forming. By the fetal period, organs already exist, growth is the main task. 3. Piaget, Cognitive Development 4 stages Stage Age Achievements Limits Sensorimotor 0-2 Object permanence (~8mo), goal-directed action, deferred imitation (end) No symbolic thought early on Preoperational 2-7 Symbolic thought, language, pretend play Egocentrism, animism, centration, no conservation Concrete Operational 7-11 Conservation, reversibility, classification, seriation, decentration Tied to concrete reality, abstract is shaky Formal Operational 11+ Abstract, hypothetico-deductive, propositional logic Adolescent egocentrism (imaginary audience, personal fable) Sensorimotor 6 substages (mini-list) Reflexive schemes (0-1mo) Primary circular reactions (1-4mo, on own body) Secondary circular reactions (4-8mo, on objects) Coordination of secondary schemes (8-12mo, intentional, object permanence , A-not-B error) Tertiary circular reactions (12-18mo, experimentation) Mental representation (18-24mo, deferred imitation, symbolic thought) Key concepts Schema — mental framework for understanding the world. Assimilation — fitting new info into existing schema (a horse = a "doggie"). Accommodation — modifying schema for new info ("ok, that's a horse, not a doggie"). Equilibration — drive to balance assimilation + accommodation, engine of cognitive change. Egocentrism — preoperational, can't take another's perspective. Three Mountains task. Animism — preoperational, attributing life to objects. Centration — focus on one feature at a time, blocks conservation. Conservation — quantity stays same despite change in form (number, mass, volume). Order: number → mass → liquid → length → area → weight → volume (last, ~11). TRAP: Object permanence (sensorimotor, ~8mo) ≠ Conservation (concrete operational, ~7yr). Different stages, different concepts. TRAP: "Egocentrism" in dev psych ≠ narcissism. It's a cognitive limit, not a personality trait. Critiques of Piaget Underestimated infants (modern habituation studies show object permanence earlier). Stages less discrete than he claimed (horizontal décalage = uneven within a stage). Underplayed culture (Vygotsky's main attack). Not everyone reaches formal operational, especially for unfamiliar content. 4. Vygotsky, Sociocultural ZPD (Zone of Proximal Development) — gap between what child can do alone vs with help from a more knowledgeable other (MKO). Scaffolding — temporary tailored support, withdrawn as competence grows. Bruner's term , applied to Vygotsky's framework. Private speech — kids talk to themselves while problem-solving. Becomes inner speech, guides cognition. Piaget called this "egocentric speech" and dismissed it; Vygotsky said it's central. Tools of thought — language is the master tool, internalized from social interaction. Higher mental functions are socially mediated . Cultural specificity — cognitive development depends on the cultural tools available (counting systems, writing, schooling). TRAP: "Scaffolding" = Bruner , not Vygotsky. Vygotsky's own terms are ZPD and MKO. Piaget vs Vygotsky in one line: Piaget = child as lone scientist (development → learning). Vygotsky = child as apprentice (learning → development, mediated by culture). 5. Bronfenbrenner, Ecological Systems / Bioecological Full standalone primer with PPCT details: notes/bronfenbrenner . Cheatsheet version below is exam-grade. Core idea Urie Bronfenbrenner (1917-2005). Development = ongoing interaction between the person and a set of nested environmental systems . Ecological Systems Theory (1979) → renamed Bioecological Model (1994) with the PPCT mechanism. Co-founded Head Start (1965). The 5 systems (innermost → outermost) System What it is Examples Microsystem Direct, face-to-face settings; bidirectional Family, school, peers, daycare Mesosystem Interactions between microsystem

title: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Pavlov) Operant (Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: both decrease a behaviour. Positive punishment Negative punishment Operation Add something aversive (scolding, spanking) Remove something pleasant (take phone, time-out, fine) Other name — Response cost / omission The tell: Positive = something was added ; negative = something was taken away . Both still reduce the behaviour, so judge by add vs subtract, not by good vs bad. Primary reinforcer vs Secondary reinforcer Same: both strengthen behaviour when they follow it. Primary Secondary (conditioned) Why it reinforces Innately satisfies a biological need (food, water, sex, warmth) Learned value through association Learning needed? No Yes (money, tokens, praise, grades) The tell: Does it satisfy a body need directly (primary) or only because you learned it stands for something else (secondary)? Money is the classic secondary reinforcer. Shaping vs Chaining Same: both build complex operant behaviour using reinforcement. Shaping Chaining What's reinforced Successive approximations to one target behaviour Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours Picture it Refining one act closer and closer Step 1 → step 2 → step 3 as a chain The tell: One behaviour polished step-by-step (shaping) vs several separate behaviours joined in order (chaining). Stimulus generalisation vs Stimulus discrimination Same: both describe how a conditioned response transfers (or doesn't) across stimuli. Generalisation Discrimination Response to similar cues Yes — spreads to stimuli like the CS No — only the exact CS triggers it Little Albert Feared all furry white things Would fear only the rat The tell: Response spreads to lookalikes (generalisation) vs narrows to one exact cue (discrimination). 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky. 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulus is present (absolute) vs detecting a difference between two

title: Genetic, Chromosomal & Metabolic Disorders
text: Genetic, Chromosomal & Metabolic Disorders High-yield for MET 2026 + NIMHANS · Built 2026-05-16 Why this page. NIMHANS and MET both ask "which disorder is associated with which gene / chromosome / enzyme / behaviour." The MCQ traps are almost always trisomy number, sex chromosome count, inheritance pattern, or the one giveaway feature (musical ear, self-mutilation, happy puppet, etc.). Memorise the table, then the traps. Three things to know per disorder: (1) genetic mechanism, (2) one physical or biochemical sign, (3) one behavioural / cognitive sign. That's the MCQ unit. 1. Master one-line table (memorise this) Disorder Mechanism One-line ID IQ / behaviour Down syndrome Trisomy 21 (47,XX/XY+21) Flat face, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, hypotonia IQ 30-70; sociable, "Prince Charming"; early-onset Alzheimer's after 40 Edwards syndrome Trisomy 18 Clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet Severe ID; <10% survive 1 year Patau syndrome Trisomy 13 Cleft lip/palate, polydactyly, holoprosencephaly Severe ID; <10% survive 1 year Klinefelter 47,XXY (extra X in males) Tall, gynecomastia, small testes, infertility Mild ID or normal; verbal < performance IQ; shy, immature Turner 45,X0 (missing X in females) Short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, amenorrhoea Normal verbal IQ, poor visuospatial;
