hand-flapping, ASD overlap Williams Microdeletion 7q11.23 (elastin gene) Elfin face, supravalvular aortic stenosis Mild-mod ID; hypersocial , "cocktail party" speech, musical affinity Prader-Willi Paternal 15q11-13 deletion (or maternal UPD) Hypotonia in infancy, hyperphagia later, obesity Mild ID, compulsive eating, skin-picking, temper outbursts Angelman Maternal 15q11-13 deletion (or paternal UPD) Ataxic gait, microcephaly, seizures Severe ID, no speech, inappropriate laughter , "happy puppet" Cri-du-chat 5p deletion (5p−) High-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism Severe ID, delayed motor + language DiGeorge / VCFS 22q11.2 deletion Cardiac defects, cleft palate, hypocalcaemia, thymic aplasia Mild ID; very high schizophrenia risk (~25×) Rett MECP2 mutation, X-linked dominant (only girls survive) Normal 6-18 mo, then deceleration of head growth Loss of purposeful hand use → stereotyped hand-wringing Huntington's CAG repeat on chr 4, autosomal dominant Chorea (involuntary jerky movements), caudate atrophy Onset 30-50; subcortical dementia; depression + suicide Wilson's ATP7B mutation, autosomal recessive (copper) Kayser-Fleischer rings, hepatic + neuro signs Behavioural change, psychosis, treatable with chelation PKU PAH enzyme deficiency, autosomal recessive Musty odour, fair skin/hair, eczema Severe ID if untreated; preventable by Phe-free diet Tay-Sachs Hexosaminidase A deficiency, autosomal recessive (Ashkenazi) Cherry-red macula , exaggerated startle Regression by 6 mo, death by 4 yr Lesch-Nyhan HGPRT deficiency, X-linked recessive (purines) Hyperuricaemia, gout Compulsive self-mutilation (lip/finger biting), aggression Galactosaemia GALT enzyme deficiency, autosomal recessive Jaundice, cataracts, hepatomegaly after milk ID if untreated; treat with lactose-free diet Maple syrup urine BCKD deficiency, autosomal recessive Sweet-smelling urine, lethargy in neonate Seizures, ID, coma if untreated Hurler / Hunter MPS storage disorders (α-L-iduronidase / iduronate sulfatase) Coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, corneal clouding Progressive ID; Hunter = X-linked, Hurler = autosomal recessive Neurofibromatosis 1 NF1 gene, chr 17, autosomal dominant Café-au-lait spots (≥6), neurofibromas, Lisch nodules Learning disability ~50%, ADHD overlap Tuberous Sclerosis TSC1 (9q) / TSC2 (16p), autosomal dominant Ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, seizures ID + autism in ~50%; high epilepsy 2. Chromosomal disorders — deeper dive 2.1 Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) Most common chromosomal cause of ID . Incidence ~1 in 700 live births overall. Mechanism (95%) : maternal non-disjunction at meiosis I. Risk rises sharply with maternal age (1/1500 at 20, 1/100 at 40, 1/30 at 45). Other 5% : Robertsonian translocation (14;21) — inheritable, recurrence risk much higher; mosaicism — milder phenotype. Physical : brachycephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots on iris, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single transverse palmar crease (simian), short fifth finger (clinodactyly), sandal-gap toe. Medical : congenital heart defect (AV septal defect, ~50%), duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, atlantoaxial instability, leukaemia risk. Cognitive/behavioural : IQ commonly 30-70 (mild to moderate ID), sociable temperament, language < comprehension, mosaic Down syndrome milder. Early-onset Alzheimer's by 40s (extra APP gene on chr 21). Screen : triple test (low AFP, high hCG, low estriol). Confirmed by karyotype. TRAP: "Translocation Down" can be inherited from a carrier parent. Non-disjunction Down is not inherited and increases with maternal age. Know which. 2.2 Klinefelter (47,XXY) Most common sex-chromosome aneuploidy (~1 in 600 males). Tall stature, long limbs, small firm testes, gynecomastia, sparse body hair, infertility (azoospermia). Cognitive: verbal IQ typically below performance IQ, language delay, reading difficulties; IQ often normal or borderline. Behavioural: shy, immature, anxious; increased risk of depression and breast cancer. Treatment: testosterone replacement at puberty. 2.3 Turner (45,X0) Only viable monosomy in humans (~1 in 2,500 females). Short stature, webbed neck, low posterior hairline, shield chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, lymphoedema of hands/feet in newborn. Streak ovaries → primary amenorrhoea, infertility;

title: Effects — every named "____ effect," who gave it, the one-line hook
text: Effects — every named "____ effect," who gave it, the one-line hook First of the four category sweeps. The bucket is "named effects." NIMHANS / MET love to give you a name and ask "who proposed it" OR describe the situation and ask you to name the effect. So each row pairs the effect → person → what it is . Read it once for the pairings, re-pass with the right column covered. Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. If the stem names "the ___ effect," the answer is usually a person (who coined it). If the stem describes a scene with no name, the answer is usually the effect . This page drills both directions. The trap is always a same-family effect (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, primacy↔recency), so learn each in its pair. Jump to: 1. Memory & learning 2. Attention & perception 3. Social & expectancy 4. Judgment & decision 5. Persuasion & media 6. Biological & clinical 1. Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Lockhart Deeper (semantic) processing → better memory than shallow (visual/acoustic). Swap-trap: remove the delay/distractor and it's the recency end that vanishes (STM decays), primacy survives. Zeigarnik = unfinished remembered; von Restorff = distinctive remembered. Don't merge them. 2. Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. NIMHANS angle: the phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are on the Phenomena page (they're called "phenomena," not "effects") — don't go looking for them here. 3. Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better. Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking. Bystander effect Latané & Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in a group than alone. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Nisbett Paying for an already-enjoyed activity kills the intrinsic motivation. Boomerang effect Hovland tradition Persuasion backfires, shifting the attitude the opposite way (cousin of reactance). Same-study, different name: Pygmalion = Rosenthal & Jacobson (high expectation lifts), Golem = low expectation drops, Hawthorne = Mayo (being watched changes behaviour). Examiners swap these three constantly. 4. Judgment & decision effects Effect Who What it is Barnum / Forer effect Bertram Forer Accepting vague, general descriptions as uniquely true of you (horoscopes, cold reading). Dunning–Kruger effect Dunning & Kruger Low-skill people overestimate their own competence. Anchoring effect Tversky & Kahneman First number seen drags later estimates toward it. Framing effect Tversky & Kahneman Same facts, different wording (gain vs loss) flips

title: Ethics in Practice — the terms they test
text: Ethics in Practice — the terms they test Each principle + what it actually looks like in the clinic room · Built 2026-05-22 How they ask this. Either straight definition ("non-maleficence means ___") or a vignette ("a clinician does X, which principle is violated?"). The 4 big ones are Beauchamp & Childress's principles . The rest are the day-to-day rules that fall out of them. For each, learn the one-line definition and the in-practice example, because the vignette items only give you the scenario. The 4 core principles (Beauchamp & Childress) Mnemonic: "A-B-N-J" / "Auto Brings No Justice." Autonomy · Beneficence · Non-maleficence · Justice. Principle One line In practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide for themselves Informed consent · right to refuse treatment · not coercing Beneficence Act for the client's good Choosing the treatment most likely to help · promoting wellbeing Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" ( primum non nocere ) Not using unproven/harmful methods · staying within competence Justice Fairness — treat like cases alike, distribute resources fairly No discrimination · fair access to care · equitable waitlists The classic swap: beneficence = do good , non-maleficence = avoid harm . They're a pair but separate principles. "Withholding a harmful drug" = non-maleficence. "Giving a helpful one" = beneficence. What falls under Autonomy Informed consent: client understands the nature, risks, benefits, and alternatives, and agrees voluntarily and with capacity . Three pillars: disclosure · capacity · voluntariness. Assent: agreement from someone who can't legally consent (a minor) — you still get their assent alongside the parent's consent . Right to refuse / withdraw at any time without penalty. Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice "for their own good." It's the violation of autonomy. Only justified when the person lacks capacity. Confidentiality and its limits Confidentiality: not disclosing client information. Privacy = the client's right; confidentiality = your duty to protect it; privileged communication = the legal protection in court. Limits / when you must break it: risk of serious harm to self or others · suspected child/elder abuse ( mandatory reporting ) · court order. Duty to warn / protect (Tarasoff): if a client makes a credible threat against an identifiable person, the therapist must act to protect that person. This is where non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. Very common vignette. The other named terms Term Means Fidelity Loyalty, keeping promises, being trustworthy and reliable to the client Veracity Truth-telling — being honest with the client (e.g. about diagnosis, prognosis) Competence Practising only within the limits of your training; refer out otherwise Dual / multiple relationship Having a second role with a client (friend, business, romantic) — a boundary violation Duty of care The legal/ethical obligation to act in the client's best interest Negligence Falling below the accepted standard of care, causing harm (basis of malpractice) Capacity / competence to consent Whether the person can understand and reason about the decision Vulnerability Extra protection owed to those who can't fully protect their own interests (children, severe MI) Indian context (worth a line) RCI (Rehabilitation Council of India) licenses clinical psychologists and has its own code of ethics . Mental Healthcare Act 2017 codifies advance directives, nominated representative, right to confidentiality, and consent for persons with mental illness, plus decriminalises suicide attempt. APA Ethics Code is the international reference (the 5 general principles: beneficence/non-maleficence, fidelity/responsibility, integrity, justice, respect for rights & dignity). Match the scenario to the principle Cover the right column, name the principle violated or upheld. Scenario Principle Therapist uses a technique they're not trained in and the client worsens Non-maleficence (+ competence) Clinician forces medication on a competent, refusing adult Autonomy violated (paternalism) Psychologist dates a current client Fidelity / dual relationship — boundary violation Therapist tells a client's threat to the named target Upholds duty to warn (Tarasoff); breaks confidentiality lawfully Same waitlist priority regardless of caste/income Justice Choosing the most evidence-based treatment for the client Beneficence Hiding a poor prognosis from the client Veracity violated Sharing case details at a party Confidentiality violated Getting a 14-year-old's agreement alongside the parent's consent Assent (+ consent) The traps Beneficence vs non-maleficence. Do good vs avoid harm. If the answer is about stopping/avoiding something harmful, it's non-maleficence. Privacy vs confidentiality vs privilege. Privacy = the right · confidentiality = your duty · privileged communication = court protection. Consent vs assent. Adults with capacity give consent ; minors give assent (parent gives consent). Autonomy vs paternalism. Overriding a competent refusal "for their good" violates autonomy. Only ok if capacity is genuinely absent. Confidentiality is not absolute. Harm to self/others, abuse reporting, and court orders override it. Tarasoff is the headline case. Companion notes : Therapy components · Full psychotherapy cheatsheet · Consolidated revision pack . Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/ethics-terms/

title: General Psychology — detailed notes
text: General Psychology — detailed notes Perception · attention · memory · learning · emotion · motivation · intelligence · cognition · landmark experiments · Built 2026-05-22 What this is. The detailed standalone general-psychology notes you asked for, one section per area, each with the named theories, the people behind them, and the traps. This is the depth; the Rapid Recall block is the one-line version for the cab. Use this to read, that one to test yourself. Jump to: 1. Perception 2. Attention 3. Memory 4. Learning 5. Emotion 6. Motivation 7. Intelligence 8. Cognition 9. Landmark experiments 10. Personality 11. Social psychology 12. Developmental 13. Consciousness & sleep 14. Stress & coping 15. Schools & history 1. Perception & Sensation Sensation is detecting raw stimulus energy at the receptors; perception is the brain organising and interpreting it. Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy into neural signals. Psychophysics (thresholds) Concept Meaning Absolute threshold Smallest intensity detectable 50 percent of the time Difference threshold (JND) Smallest change between two stimuli that is detectable 50 percent of the time Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the stimulus, not a fixed amount Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (often fits better than Fechner) Subliminal / priming Stimuli below the absolute threshold can still prime responses Signal detection theory Detection is a decision under uncertainty, not a fixed threshold. Four outcomes: hit , miss , false alarm , correct rejection . d-prime (d') measures true sensitivity; beta is the response criterion (how willing you are to say "yes"). Motivation and expectation shift beta, not sensitivity. Theories of perception The two camps: Gibson's direct / bottom-up theory (the stimulus itself carries enough information, perception is data-driven) versus Gregory's constructivist / top-down theory (perception is an active hypothesis built from prior knowledge and inference). Most modern views combine both. Gestalt laws of organisation "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts." Proximity, similarity, closure, continuity (good continuation), common fate, figure-ground, pragnanz (simplicity). Founders: Wertheimer, Koffka, Kohler. Depth & constancy Binocular cues: retinal disparity, convergence. Monocular cues: relative size, interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, motion parallax, aerial perspective. Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness, the object looks stable despite changing retinal image. Feature integration theory (Treisman): a preattentive stage detects individual features in parallel, then focused attention binds them into a whole object. Failure of binding produces illusory conjunctions. Pattern recognition & perceptual set Template, prototype, and feature-detection theories of how we recognise patterns; Biederman's recognition-by-components (geons) builds objects from basic 3D primitives. Perceptual set / expectancy: context, motivation, culture, and prior knowledge bias what we perceive (top-down). Illusions: Müller-Lyer, Ponzo, Ames room, moon illusion, the Kanizsa triangle (illusory contours), the McGurk effect (vision alters what we hear). Illusions reveal the brain's interpretive shortcuts. 2. Attention Attention is the selective allocation of limited processing capacity. The big debate: where in the stream does selection happen (early vs late), and how much capacity is there (bottleneck vs flexible resources). Bottleneck / filter models (where does selection happen?) Model Claim Broadbent (1958, early selection) A single filter blocks unattended input early , based on physical features (pitch, location), before meaning is processed. Based on Cherry's dichotic-listening / shadowing work. Treisman (1964, attenuation) The filter attenuates (turns down) unattended input rather than fully blocking it; high-priority words with low thresholds (your name, "fire") still break through. Deutsch & Deutsch / Norman (late selection) All input is fully processed for meaning; selection happens late , at the response/awareness stage, not at perception. Johnston & Heinz (multimode) Selection is flexible: it can occur early or late depending on task demands, but later selection costs more capacity. Capacity / resource models (how much is there?) Model Claim Kahneman (1973, single capacity) Attention is one limited pool of effort/resources allocated across tasks; arousal changes the size of the pool; an allocation policy decides where it goes. Wickens (multiple resources) There are several separate resource pools (e.g. visual vs auditory, verbal vs spatial). Two tasks interfere most when they draw on the same pool, which is why you can drive and listen but not read and listen. Norman & Bobrow Data-limited (limited by poor stimulus quality) vs resource-limited (limited by available attention) performance. Lavie (perceptual load theory) Under high perceptual load selection is early (no spare capacity, distractors filtered out); under low load spare capacity spills onto distractors, so selection is late. Reconciles the early/late debate. Spatial / visual attention Spotlight model (Posner): attention is a movable "spotlight" that enhances processing wherever it points. Zoom-lens (Eriksen): the spotlight can widen or narrow, trading area for resolution. Posner cueing paradigm: a valid cue speeds detection, an invalid one slows it. Endogenous (voluntary, goal-driven, central cue) vs exogenous (reflexive, stimulus-driven, peripheral cue) orienting. Phases of orienting: disengage → move → engage. Feature Integration Theory (Treisman): a preattentive stage registers features (colour, orientation) in parallel across the field; focused attention then binds them into objects. Feature search ("pop-out") is parallel and fast; conjunction search is serial. Failed binding = illusory conjunctions . Guid

text: High-Yield Revision Sheet Abnormal + Developmental Psychology · Built 2026-05-04 · 19 days to MET How to use this sheet. One pass tonight, full read. One pass tomorrow morning, only the red TRAP boxes and the tables. Anything you blank on, mark it and re-read the corresponding cheatsheet section. Don't try to memorize this in one sitting, target the gaps. 1. Abnormal Psychology 1.1 The 4 Ds (definition of abnormality) Deviance — statistical or social norm violation Distress — subjective suffering Dysfunction — impairs daily life / role functioning Danger — risk to self or others TRAP: Deviance alone ≠ abnormal. A genius IQ is statistically deviant but not pathological. Always need distress or dysfunction with it. 1.2 Historical conceptions, one-line Era Model Key name Ancient Supernatural (demons, possession) Trephination Greek Biological, four humors Hippocrates Middle Ages Demonological return, witch trials Malleus Maleficarum Renaissance Asylum reform begins Pinel (moral treatment), Tuke 19th c. Biological / classification Kraepelin (dementia praecox), Bleuler (renamed schizophrenia) 20th c. Psychological Freud (psychoanalysis), Watson (behaviorism), Beck (CBT) 1.3 DSM-5 vs ICD-11, must-knows DSM-5 (2013) / DSM-5-TR (2022) ICD-11 (2019) Publisher APA, US WHO, global Sections 3 sections, 22 chapters, no axes (axes dropped from DSM-IV) Chapter 6 = mental, behavioral, neurodev OCD Own chapter (separated from anxiety) Own chapter too PTSD Own chapter (Trauma-related) Own chapter, adds Complex PTSD Schizophrenia subtypes Removed in DSM-5 (no more paranoid/catatonic/etc.) Removed in ICD-11 too Mental Retardation Renamed Intellectual Developmental Disorder Disorders of Intellectual Development Asperger's Folded into ASD Folded into ASD Bereavement exclusion (MDD) Removed Still cautious TRAP: Multi-axial system was DSM-IV. DSM-5 dropped it. If a question says "Axis I disorder" it is testing pre-DSM-5 vocabulary. 1.4 Mental Status Examination (MSE), order matters ABS-MTPCIJ : Appearance, Behavior, Speech, Mood/affect, Thought (form + content), Perception, Cognition, Insight, Judgment. Mood = subjective ("how do you feel"). Affect = observed (range, congruence). Thought form = how thoughts flow (loose, tangential, flight of ideas, circumstantial). Thought content = what (delusions, suicidal, obsessions). Insight = awareness of illness. Judgment = decision-making in real situations. 1.5 Approaches to psychopathology Approach Cause Treatment Biological Genes, neurotransmitters, brain Meds, ECT Psychodynamic Unconscious conflict, early experience Psychoanalysis, free association Behavioral Maladaptive learning Conditioning, exposure, reinforcement Cognitive Distorted thoughts, schemas CBT, cognitive restructuring (Beck, Ellis) Humanistic Blocked self-actualization Person-centered (Rogers), Gestalt (Perls) Sociocultural Family, culture, stigma Family therapy, community Biopsychosocial All three interact (Engel, 1977) Integrative 1.6 Anxiety disorders, distinguishing features Disorder Core feature Time GAD Excessive worry, multiple domains, hard to control ≥ 6 months Panic Disorder Recurrent unexpected panic attacks + worry about more Attack peaks in 10 min Specific Phobia Fear of one object/situation ≥ 6 months Social Anxiety Fear of scrutiny, judgment in social situations ≥ 6 months Agoraphobia Fear of places where escape is hard (≥ 2 of 5 situations) ≥ 6 months Separation Anxiety Excessive fear of separation from attachment figure ≥ 4 wks (kids), 6 mo (adults) TRAP: OCD is NOT in the anxiety chapter in DSM-5. It has its own chapter (OCD and related). Same for PTSD (Trauma- and stressor-related). 1.7 OCD and related, hoard the list OCD Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) Hoarding Disorder (new in DSM-5) Trichotillomania (hair-pulling) Excoriation (skin-picking, new in DSM-5) 1.8 Mood disorders Disorder Episode Duration MDD ≥ 5 of 9 SIG-E-CAPS, must include depressed mood OR anhedonia ≥ 2 weeks Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) Chronic low-grade depression ≥ 2 yrs (1 yr kids) Bipolar I ≥ 1 manic episode (depression not required) Mania ≥ 1 wk Bipolar II Hypomania + at least one MDE, no full mania ever Hypomania ≥ 4 days Cyclothymia Hypomanic + depressive symptoms, never full episode ≥ 2 yrs PMDD Severe mood symptoms premenstrually Most cycles in last yr Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder Severe temper outbursts in kids Onset before 10, dx 6-18 SIG-E-CAPS for MDD: Sleep, Interest (anhedonia), Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal ideation. + depressed mood = 9 total. DIG-FAST for mania: Distractibility, Indiscretion, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep decrease, Talkativeness. 1.9 Suicide risk, SAD PERSONS S ex (male), A ge (<19 or >45), D epression, P revious attempt, E thanol/drugs, R ational thinking loss, S ocial supports lacking, O rganized plan, N o spouse, S ickness. TRAP: Strongest single predictor of completed suicide = previous attempt . Most common method globally = hanging. Highest-risk diagnosis = MDD with comorbid substance use. 1.10 Schizophrenia (Schneider, Bleuler, DSM-5) Bleuler's 4 As : Associations (loose), Affect (flat), Ambivalence, Autism (withdrawal). Schneider's First-Rank Symptoms : thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, audible thoughts, voices commenting/arguing, made impulses/actions, somatic passivity, delusional perception. Suggestive but not diagnostic alone. Positive symptoms : hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior. Negative symptoms : flat affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality. DSM-5 criteria : ≥ 2 of (delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms), at least one from first three. Active phase ≥ 1 month, total disturbance ≥ 6 months. title: HPA Axis — Stress Endocrinology
text: HPA Axis — Stress Endocrinology Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal axis · Built 2026-05-16 Why this matters. HPA shows up in MET + NIMHANS papers under at least four hats: (1) biopsych "draw the axis," (2) abnormal psych "HPA in MDD/PTSD/Cushing's," (3) stress/health psych "Selye + allostatic load," (4) assessment "dexamethasone suppression test." One page, all four. Three things to know cold: CRH → ACTH → cortisol, the negative feedback loop, and which psychiatric disorder shows what kind of HPA dysregulation. 1. The axis in one diagram STRESSOR (physical, psychological, immune) ↓ HYPOTHALAMUS (paraventricular nucleus, PVN) → releases CRH (Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone) + AVP (vasopressin, synergistic) ↓ (via portal blood, infundibular stalk) ANTERIOR PITUITARY (corticotroph cells) → releases ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) from POMC precursor ↓ (via systemic circulation) ADRENAL CORTEX — zona fasciculata → releases CORTISOL (glucocorticoid) + small DHEA, weak aldosterone ↓ TARGET TISSUES : liver, muscle, fat, immune, brain NEGATIVE FEEDBACK : cortisol inhibits both hypothalamus (↓CRH) and pituitary (↓ACTH). This loop shuts the response off when the stressor ends. In MDD and PTSD it breaks. 1.1 Anatomy details to memorise Paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of hypothalamus — the brain origin of stress. CRH = 41-amino-acid peptide, half-life ~60 min. Co-secreted with AVP (potentiates). Anterior pituitary corticotrophs make POMC → cleaved to ACTH + β-endorphin + MSH. Adrenal cortex layers (outside in): G lomerulosa (aldosterone), F asciculata (cortisol), R eticularis (androgens — DHEA). Memory: " GFR , salt-sugar-sex deeper you go". Adrenal medulla (inner) makes adrenaline / noradrenaline via SAM axis — fast, "fight-or-flight". HPA is the slower, sustained arm. 2. The two stress systems (compare and contrast) SAM (Sympatho-Adrenal Medullary) HPA Onset Seconds Minutes Hormones Adrenaline, noradrenaline Cortisol (with CRH, ACTH) Source Adrenal medulla, sympathetic neurons Adrenal cortex, via hypothalamus + pituitary Effect ↑HR, ↑BP, pupil dilation, bronchodilation, blood to muscle ↑glucose, ↑BP sustained, ↓immune, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑lipolysis Role Immediate fight-or-flight Sustained mobilisation + recovery Cannon vs Selye Cannon's "fight or flight" Selye's GAS, "stress" coined 3. Cortisol — what it actually does Metabolic : ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑glycogenolysis, ↑lipolysis, ↑proteolysis (catabolic). Raises blood glucose. Immune : suppresses inflammation, decreases lymphocytes, neutrophilia. That's why glucocorticoids are anti-inflammatory drugs. Cardiovascular : maintains vascular tone, permissive for catecholamines. CNS : alertness, attention. At chronic high levels: hippocampal atrophy, memory deficits, mood changes. GI : ↑gastric acid (chronic stress → ulcers). Bone : ↑resorption, ↓formation → osteoporosis with chronic excess. 3.1 Cortisol's diurnal rhythm Peak : ~30 min after waking ("cortisol awakening response", CAR). Trough : around midnight. Tightly tied to SCN (suprachiasmatic nucleus) circadian rhythm via the hypothalamus. Disrupted in shift workers, depression, chronic insomnia, jet lag. 4. HPA dysregulation in psychiatric disorders 4.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) Hyperactive HPA axis is one of the most replicated biological findings in MDD. Elevated baseline cortisol; blunted diurnal variation; flattened cortisol awakening response. Enlarged adrenal glands on imaging. Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST) : give 1 mg dex at 11 pm, measure cortisol next morning. In healthy subjects → cortisol suppressed. In ~50% of melancholic / psychotic depression → non-suppression . Sensitivity ~40-50%, specificity ~80-90%, not used diagnostically but historically big in NIMHANS papers (Carroll DST). Mechanism: impaired glucocorticoid receptor feedback → cortisol cannot turn the axis off → sustained CRH drive. Reduces hippocampal BDNF, contributes to volume loss. SSRIs and CBT both normalise HPA over weeks of treatment. 4.2 PTSD — paradox PTSD shows low basal cortisol (often) but enhanced negative feedback (super-suppression on low-dose DST). Elevated CRH in CSF. Theory: hypersensitive glucocorticoid receptors → over-suppression of cortisol after stressor. Contrast with MDD: depressed = hypercortisolaemic with failed feedback; PTSD = hypocortisolaemic with exaggerated feedback. Frequent MCQ trap. 4.3 Cushing's syndrome / disease Excess cortisol from any cause. Cushing's disease = pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma (most common endogenous cause). Cushing's syndrome = the broader phenotype, often iatrogenic (exogenous steroids). Physical: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hirsutism, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, thin skin, easy bruising. Psychiatric: depression in 50-80% , irritability, anxiety, insomnia, occasional psychosis or mania. Treating the Cushing's often resolves the depression — pure example of endocrine psychiatry. 4.4 Addison's disease Primary adrenal insufficiency — cortisol and aldosterone deficient. Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation (high ACTH stimulates MSH), hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia. Psychiatric: apathy, depression, occasional psychosis. Reverses with hydrocortisone replacement. 4.5 Anxiety disorders, panic, OCD Findings are mixed. Panic disorder shows mild HPA activation during attacks but normal baselines. GAD: subtle blunting of CAR, elevated evening cortisol. OCD: no clear HPA signature — less examinable than mood / PTSD. 4.6 Schizophrenia HPA hyperactivity at first episode, especially with poor outcome. Cortisol rises before psychotic relapse in some prospective studies. Linked to dopamine sensitisation theory ("threat → cortisol → mesolimbic DA"). 4.7 Eating disorders Anorexia nervosa: hypercortisolaemia, loss of diurnal variation, often DST non-suppression even without depression. Restoration of weight partly normalises HPA. 4.8 Early life stress / abuse Childhood maltreatment → durable HPA dysregulation in adulthood (often blunted r

title: ICD — the full breakdown
text: ICD — the full breakdown International Classification of Diseases: who owns it, how it's built, ICD-10 vs ICD-11, the F-codes for mental disorders, and every place it differs from DSM. Built 2026-05-24. Read the boxes and tables; the prose is just glue. One-line frame. The ICD is the WHO's global classification of all diseases, not just mental ones. Mental disorders sit in one chapter of it. DSM (American Psychiatric Association) only does mental disorders. So: ICD = whole-body, global, free, used for official health stats; DSM = mental-only, US, paywalled, used heavily in research. NIMHANS/India officially uses ICD . Jump to: 1. What ICD is & who owns it 2. Version history 3. Where mental disorders live 4. ICD-10 F-codes (F00–F99) 5. ICD-11 & what changed 6. ICD vs DSM 7. Exam traps 1. What ICD is & who owns it Question Answer Full name International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems Who publishes it WHO (World Health Organization). DSM is APA, the contrast they love. Scope All diseases and health conditions, every body system. Mental & behavioural disorders are just one chapter . Purpose Global standard for mortality & morbidity statistics , billing, epidemiology. It's the official tool for cause-of-death and disease reporting worldwide. Cost Free , multilingual. DSM is copyrighted and sold by APA. Used where ~194 WHO member states, including India . DSM dominates US clinical research. 2. Version history (the dates they ask) Version Year Note ICD-6 1949 First edition to include a section on mental disorders. Common MCQ. ICD-8 1965 ICD-9 1975 US used a clinical modification, ICD-9-CM , for decades. ICD-10 1990 endorsed, 1992 in use The one still tested. Mental disorders = Chapter V (F-codes) . Alphanumeric coding introduced here. ICD-11 Adopted 2019, in force 1 Jan 2022 Fully digital, "foundation" architecture. Mental disorders = Chapter 06 . Lock: ICD-6 (1949) = first mental-disorder section · ICD-10 (1992) = F-codes · ICD-11 (in force 2022) = current. 3. Where mental disorders live ICD-10 ICD-11 Chapter Chapter V Chapter 06 Title Mental and Behavioural Disorders Mental, Behavioural or Neurodevelopmental Disorders Code prefix F (F00–F99) Alphanumeric 6 -codes (e.g. 6A20 for schizophrenia) Companion text "Blue Book" (Clinical Descriptions & Diagnostic Guidelines) + "Green Book" (research criteria) CDDR (Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements) Why "F"? No mnemonic meaning, it's just the letter assigned to the mental-disorders chapter (Chapter V) in ICD-10's alphanumeric scheme. If asked "F-codes refer to," answer mental and behavioural disorders . 4. ICD-10 F-codes — the F00–F99 blocks (memorise the ranges) Range Block Examples F00–F09 Organic, incl. symptomatic, mental disorders Dementia (Alzheimer's, vascular), delirium F10–F19 Mental/behavioural due to psychoactive substance use Alcohol, opioids, cannabis dependence F20–F29 Schizophrenia , schizotypal & delusional disorders Schizophrenia (F20), delusional disorder F30–F39 Mood (affective) disorders Mania, bipolar, depression, recurrent depressive F40–F48 Neurotic, stress-related & somatoform Phobias, panic, GAD, OCD, PTSD, dissociative, somatoform F50–F59 Behavioural syndromes + physiological/physical factors Eating disorders, sleep disorders, sexual dysfunction F60–F69 Disorders of adult personality & behaviour Personality disorders, gender identity, habit/impulse F70–F79 Mental retardation (ICD-10 term; "intellectual disability" in ICD-11) Mild → profound F80–F89 Disorders of psychological development Speech/language, scholastic, autism (F84) F90–F98 Behavioural/emotional onset usually in childhood/adolescence ADHD/hyperkinetic (F90), conduct, tic disorders F99 Unspecified mental disorder Trap they set: In ICD-10, OCD and PTSD sit inside F40–F48 (neurotic/stress-related), NOT as standalone chapters. That's the opposite of DSM-5, which pulled OCD and trauma out into their own chapters. Know which manual the question is about. Fast recall: 0 organic · 1 substances · 2 schizophrenia · 3 mood · 4 neurotic/anxiety · 5 physiological (eat/sleep/sex) · 6 personality · 7 retardation · 8 development · 9 childhood-onset. 5. ICD-11 — what actually changed Coding format changed. Mental disorders moved from F-codes to alphanumeric 6-codes (chapter 06). E.g. schizophrenia = 6A20 , bipolar type I = 6A60. Complex PTSD added. ICD-11 has PTSD AND Complex PTSD (PTSD core + the three "disturbances in self-organization": affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship disturbance). DSM-5 does not have Complex PTSD. High-yield difference. Gaming disorder added as a formal diagnosis. "Mental retardation" → "Disorders of intellectual development." Gender incongruence moved out of the mental disorders chapter into a new sexual-health chapter (depathologised). Schizophrenia subtypes removed (paranoid, catatonic, etc. dropped), matching DSM-5. Rated by symptom dimensions instead. Bereavement → Prolonged grief disorder recognised. Neurodevelopmental added to the chapter title; autism + ADHD grouped here. Dimensional personality model: ICD-11 scrapped the categorical PD types and uses severity + five trait domains (negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, anankastia) with one retained pattern, borderline . 6. ICD vs DSM — the side-by-side they ask ICD (ICD-11) DSM (DSM-5/5-TR) Body WHO APA (American Psychiatric Association) Scope All diseases; mental = 1 chapter Mental disorders only Reach Global, ~194 countries US-centric (heavy in research) Cost Free Sold/copyrighted Style Clinical guidelines (flexible, prototype-based) Explicit operational criteria (count symptoms, thresholds) Latest ICD-11, in force 2022 DSM-5 (2013), DSM-5-TR (2022) Complex PTSD Yes No Multiaxial? Never multiaxial DSM-IV had 5 axes; DSM-5 dropped axes NIMHANS angle: India officially codes on ICD . Expect "which body publishes ICD" (WHO), "ICD chapter for mental disorders" (V / F-codes in ICD-10), and an ICD-vs-DSM d

title: Intelligence Tests, Deep Reference
text: Intelligence Tests, Deep Reference Built 2026-05-20, companion to the personality + projective deep reference . Same job, different test family: for every individual + group + infant intelligence scale in the MET/NIMHANS pool, lock the item/subtest count, scales/indices, scoring, author + year, and age range . Cross-link with the read-first primer (reliability/validity/IQ history) and the revision pack (one-page table). How MCQ-writers attack intelligence tests. Five recurring moves: (1) swap the SD between Wechsler (15) and old Binet (16); (2) swap subtest count between SPM/CPM/APM, or between Bhatia (5) and Army Beta (7); (3) swap the year (Binet-Simon 1905 vs Terman 1916 vs Stern's IQ formula 1912); (4) swap which index belongs to which Wechsler version (WAIS-IV has 4, WISC-V has 5); (5) swap a theorist with their model (Spearman g, Thurstone PMA, Guilford SOI, Gardner MI, Sternberg triarchic, Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc). Memorize those five swaps cold. 1. Stanford-Binet Family Origin: Binet-Simon (1905, France) Authors: Alfred Binet & Théodore Simon, commissioned by the French Ministry of Public Instruction to identify children needing special schooling. Year: 1905 (original 30-item scale), revised 1908 (introduced mental-age concept) and 1911 . Items: 30 tasks of graded difficulty in the 1905 version. Range from "follow a light with eyes" to "abstract definitions." Key contribution: the concept of mental age (MA) in the 1908 revision - child's performance level matched to the average chronological age that performs at that level. Did NOT yield IQ. Binet himself rejected a single global score; he wanted a clinical descriptive profile. Stanford revisions - the IQ-formula era 1916 - Stanford-Binet, 1st edition. Lewis M. Terman, Stanford University. First English-language adaptation. Adopted William Stern's 1912 ratio IQ formula : IQ = (MA / CA) × 100. Mean ≈ 100. 1937 - SB-LM (2nd edition). Terman & Maud Merrill. Two equivalent forms L and M. Still ratio IQ. 1960 - SB-LM revised (3rd edition). Terman & Merrill. Switched from ratio IQ to deviation IQ (Pinneau's tables): M = 100, SD = 16 . Memorize this 16 - it is the classic Wechsler-vs-Binet trap. 1986 - SB-IV (4th edition). Thorndike, Hagen & Sattler. First time the test moved to a hierarchical structure with 4 area scores: Verbal Reasoning, Abstract/Visual Reasoning, Quantitative Reasoning, Short-Term Memory. 15 subtests. Age 2 to adult. 2003 - SB-5 (current edition). Gale H. Roid, Riverside Publishing. SD changed to 15 to align with Wechsler. Age range 2 to 85+ . SB-5 structure (the version exam-writers mean today) 10 subtests, 5 factors × 2 domains. 5 factors: Fluid Reasoning (FR), Knowledge (KN), Quantitative Reasoning (QR), Visual-Spatial Processing (VS), Working Memory (WM). Identical names across the verbal and nonverbal domains. 2 domains: Verbal (5 subtests) and Nonverbal (5 subtests). Each factor has one verbal + one nonverbal subtest. 3 IQ scores yielded: Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ), Verbal IQ (VIQ), Nonverbal IQ (NVIQ). All M = 100, SD = 15. Routing subtests: Object Series/Matrices (nonverbal) and Vocabulary (verbal) determine entry difficulty for the rest. Administration time: ~45–75 min full battery; 15–20 min abbreviated. 2. Wechsler Family David Wechsler (Bellevue Hospital, NY) built his scales explicitly to fix two SB problems: (a) it was age-stratified and clunky for adults, and (b) ratio IQ broke down past age 16 because MA stops climbing linearly. His fix was the deviation IQ (1939) and a point-scale structure where every adult takes the same subtests. Edition lineage Wechsler-Bellevue I (W-B I, 1939) - David Wechsler. First deviation-IQ test. 11 subtests. W-B II (1946) - alternate form. WAIS (1955) - adults 16–64. WAIS-R (1981) - restandardised. WAIS-III (1997) - added Processing Speed Index, 4-index structure introduced. WAIS-IV (2008) - current MET/NIMHANS reference; ages 16:0–90:11. WAIS-5 (2024) - rolled out in US/UK; exams still default to WAIS-IV unless otherwise specified. WISC (1949) → WISC-R (1974) → WISC-III (1991) → WISC-IV (2003) → WISC-V (2014 US, 2016 UK, 2019 India adaptation) . Ages 6:0–16:11. WPPSI (1967) → WPPSI-R (1989) → WPPSI-III (2002) → WPPSI-IV (2012) . Ages 2:6–7:7. WAIS-IV - the canonical exam answer Age range: 16:0 to 90:11. Total subtests: 15 (10 core + 5 supplemental). 4 index scores (memorize): Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Perceptual Reasoning (PRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). FSIQ derived from the 10 core subtests across these 4 indices. Subtest scaled scores: M = 10, SD = 3, range 1–19. FSIQ and index scores: M = 100, SD = 15. Administration time: ~60–90 minutes for FSIQ. WAIS-IV subtest map (core in bold, supplemental in italics): Index Subtests VCI Similarities, Vocabulary, Information , Comprehension PRI Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles , Figure Weights, Picture Completion WMI Digit Span, Arithmetic , Letter-Number Sequencing PSI Symbol Search, Coding , Cancellation WISC-V - the children's scale Age range: 6:0 to 16:11. Total subtests: 21 (10 primary + 11 secondary, including 5 complementary subtests scored separately). 5 primary indices: Verbal Comprehension (VCI), Visual Spatial (VSI), Fluid Reasoning (FRI), Working Memory (WMI), Processing Speed (PSI). The big WISC-IV → WISC-V change was splitting old PRI into VSI + FRI , giving 5 primary indices instead of 4. 5 ancillary indices: Quantitative Reasoning Index (QRI), Auditory Working Memory Index (AWMI), Nonverbal Index (NVI), General Ability Index (GAI), Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI). 5 complementary subtests (CHC narrow abilities): Naming Speed Literacy, Naming Speed Quantity, Immediate Symbol Translation, Delayed Symbol Translation, Recognition Symbol Translation. text: Learning & Conditioning — Full Terms Page Built 2026-05-16 because MET / NIMHANS love the operant-conditioning vocabulary as 1-mark definition traps. Every term has the same 3-row block: Definition · Classic example · MCQ trap . Skim once, then drill by closing the example/trap columns and self-quizzing on the term name. 0. Big picture — where each term sits Family Terms inside Classical (Pavlovian) phenomena Extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalization, discrimination, habituation, sensitization Operant (Skinnerian) shaping tools Shaping, chaining, fading, prompting Operant schedules FR, VR, FI, VI Cognitive / social learning Latent learning (Tolman), insight learning (Köhler), observational learning (Bandura) Implicit / cognitive priming Priming (semantic, perceptual, affective) Read this once: all of classical conditioning is about stimulus pairings , all of operant is about consequences shaping voluntary behaviour , priming is about one stimulus making a later stimulus easier to process , and habituation/sensitization are non-associative (single stimulus, no pairing). If a question mixes the families, the answer is almost always the term whose family matches the stem. 1. Priming Definition Exposure to one stimulus (the prime ) unconsciously influences the response to a later stimulus (the target ), by activating related representations in memory. A form of implicit memory. Classic example You read the word NURSE . A moment later you identify DOCTOR faster than an unrelated word like BREAD . The semantic network around "medical" was pre-activated. MCQ trap Priming is not classical conditioning — there is no UCS, no reflex, no pairing. It is also not recall — the person doesn't consciously remember the prime. Tested on the implicit-vs-explicit memory split. Subtypes: semantic (NURSE → DOCTOR), perceptual (briefly flashed word → faster identification), affective (smiling face → positive judgement). 2. Shaping Definition Reinforcing successive approximations of a target behaviour the organism doesn't yet emit. Operant, Skinner. Classic example Training a rat to press a lever: first reinforce facing the lever, then approaching it, then touching it, then pressing it. Each step gets closer to the final behaviour. MCQ trap Shaping is for behaviours the organism cannot yet do . Don't confuse with chaining (linking behaviours the organism already does into a sequence) or prompting (cueing an existing behaviour). The reinforcement criterion changes across trials — that is the defining feature. 3. Chaining Definition Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours into a longer chain, where each behaviour serves as the discriminative stimulus (S D ) for the next, and only the final link is reinforced. Classic example Brushing teeth: pick up brush → wet it → apply paste → brush → rinse → put brush away. Each step cues the next. Used heavily in ABA / autism skill training. MCQ trap Two variants — forward chaining teaches step 1 first; backward chaining teaches the last step first (so the learner always experiences the reinforcer at the natural endpoint). Backward chaining is often preferred clinically because the final reinforcer is reached immediately. Do not confuse with shaping — chaining links existing behaviours; shaping builds a new one. 4. Fading Definition Gradually removing a prompt while transferring stimulus control to the natural cue, so the behaviour eventually occurs without the prompt. Classic example Teaching a child to say "ball" — start with full verbal model ("say ball"), fade to partial ("say buh…"), fade to just holding up the ball. The picture/object becomes the controlling stimulus. MCQ trap Fading is about removing the prompt , not the reinforcer . Removing the reinforcer is extinction . Fading transfers stimulus control; extinction eliminates the behaviour. Both can run side-by-side but they target different things. 5. Prompting Definition Providing an additional stimulus (verbal, gestural, physical, modelled, visual) that helps the learner emit the correct response in the presence of the natural cue. Classic example Therapist says "wave bye-bye" and physically guides the child's hand (physical prompt). Over trials, prompts are faded until the verbal cue alone works. MCQ trap Know the prompt hierarchy from most to least intrusive: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual/positional . "Least-to-most" vs "most-to-least" prompting are common clinical-vignette distractors. Prompts are antecedent manipulations; reinforcement is a consequence — that distinction has been tested. 6. Extinction Definition Reduction and eventual disappearance of a conditioned response when reinforcement (operant) or the UCS (classical) is no longer presented. Classic example Classical: Pavlov's dog stops salivating to the bell once the bell is repeatedly presented without food. Operant: a child stops tantrumming after parents consistently ignore tantrums that previously got attention. MCQ trap Watch for the extinction burst — a temporary increase in the behaviour's frequency and intensity right after reinforcement is withdrawn, before it declines. Extinction does not erase the learning; the response can return as spontaneous recovery . Behaviours on variable schedules are most resistant to extinction (partial-reinforcement extinction effect). 7. Spontaneous Recovery Definition Reappearance of a previously extinguished conditioned response after a rest period, without any new conditioning trials. Classic example Pavlov extinguished salivation to a bell. He let the dog rest for several hours, presented the bell again, and the salivation came back (weaker than original, but real). MCQ trap Spontaneous recovery proves extinction is not unlearning — the original association is suppressed, not erased. The recovered response is typically weaker than the original. Language 6 15 Grammar fundamentals + RC tone. Assessment 4 15 IQ bands + projective trivia + z/percentile. Therapy 4 15 School-attribution traps (who does what). Biopsych (6) Language (6) Assessment (4) Therapy (4) Biostats (3) Developmental (3) Abnormal (2) Compact cheats Biopsychology, 6 wrong Pattern: you keep losing points on where structures are and which side does what . Memorise the locations, then the lesions follow. m1_bio03 Biopsych The corticospinal tract decussates primarily at the: a) Optic chiasm b) Spinal cord at the level of entry c) Pons ← you picked d) Pyramids of the medulla ← correct You: c Correct: d Why d. 85-90% of corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla, forming the lateral corticospinal tract . The remaining ~10% stay ipsilateral as the anterior corticospinal tract and cross only at the spinal segmental level. Adjacent topics they will retest: Optic chiasm (option a) crosses only the nasal retinal fibres so each cortex sees the contralateral visual field. Sectioning it = bitemporal hemianopia . Sensory decussations: dorsal column / medial lemniscus (fine touch, proprioception) crosses at the medulla (internal arcuate fibres). Spinothalamic (pain, temp) crosses at the spinal cord level of entry , 1-2 segments up. Brown-Sequard syndrome = hemisection of cord. Ipsilateral motor + dorsal column loss below the lesion, contralateral pain/temp loss starting 1-2 segments below. UMN vs LMN signs: UMN lesion (above anterior horn) = spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski up. LMN = flaccid, atrophy, fasciculations, areflexia. m1_bio05 Biopsych guessed Damage to the ventromedial hypothalamus typically produces: a) Aphagia and weight loss ← you picked b) Insomnia c) Hyperphagia and obesity ← correct d) Loss of thermoregulation You: a Correct: c Why c. VMH = satiety centre. Lesion it and you lose the "stop eating" signal → hyperphagia + obesity (the classic Hetherington-Ranson rat). You flipped it: aphagia and weight loss come from the lateral hypothalamus (LH = hunger centre) being damaged. Hypothalamus nuclei, lock these in: VMH = satiety. Lesion → hyperphagia, obesity . LH = hunger / arousal. Lesion → aphagia, lethargy . Anterior hypothalamus = cooling (parasympathetic-leaning). Lesion → hyperthermia. Posterior hypothalamus = heating. Lesion → poikilothermia (can't maintain temp). SCN (suprachiasmatic) = circadian master clock, entrained by retinohypothalamic light input. Supraoptic + paraventricular = ADH and oxytocin via the posterior pituitary. Arcuate = dopamine to anterior pituitary, plus appetite (NPY/AgRP and POMC neurons). Mammillary bodies = memory; damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff (thiamine deficiency). m1_bio06 Biopsych Which of the following is NOT a basal ganglia structure? a) Caudate nucleus b) Globus pallidus c) Red nucleus ← correct (NOT basal ganglia) d) Subthalamic nucleus ← you picked You: d Correct: c Why c. The red nucleus is in the midbrain tegmentum (origin of the rubrospinal tract, motor coordination). It is not basal ganglia. Subthalamic nucleus IS basal ganglia, that's the trap you fell into. Basal ganglia, full inventory: Striatum = caudate + putamen. Input nucleus. Globus pallidus (internal + external segments). Output via GPi. Subthalamic nucleus (STN) . Drives the indirect pathway. Substantia nigra = pars compacta (dopamine to striatum, lost in Parkinson's) + pars reticulata (output, like GPi). Lesion patterns to memorise: Parkinson's = SNc dopamine loss → rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability. Huntington's = caudate atrophy (medium spiny neurons) → chorea + cognitive decline. STN lesion = hemiballismus (wild flinging movements of contralateral limbs). Wilson's disease = copper deposition in putamen → movement + psychiatric signs. m1_bio07 Biopsych The cones of the human retina are MOST concentrated in the: a) Optic disc b) Peripheral retina ← you picked c) Fovea centralis ← correct d) Macula but not the fovea You: b Correct: c Why c. The fovea is almost exclusively cones, packed at maximum density, giving you sharpest acuity and colour. Rods dominate the periphery. The optic disc has neither = blind spot. Vision quick reference: Rods : ~120 million, peripheral, low light, no colour, slow, rhodopsin pigment. Cones : ~6 million, foveal, bright light, colour (S/M/L = blue/green/red), fast. Trichromatic theory (Young-Helmholtz) = receptor-level. Opponent-process theory (Hering) = ganglion-cell-level (red-green, blue-yellow, black-white). Lateral inhibition via horizontal/amacrine cells → edge enhancement (Mach bands). Visual pathway : retina → optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → LGN of thalamus → V1 (Brodmann 17, calcarine sulcus). Dorsal stream (where/how, parietal) vs ventral stream (what, temporal → fusiform face area for prosopagnosia). m1_bio13 Biopsych A patient with damage to the right parietal lobe is most likely to show: a) Broca's aphasia b) Anterograde amnesia c) Hemispatial neglect of the left side ← correct d) Prosopagnosia ← you picked You: d Correct: c Why c. Right inferior parietal (esp. supramarginal/angular) lesions classically cause left hemispatial neglect — the patient ignores the left side of space, eats food only on the right of the plate, fails to draw the left half of a clock. Prosopagnosia = bilateral or right fusiform (temporo-occipital), not parietal. Lob

text: MPhil Mock Review + Your Coverage Gaps An honest read on the PsychEntrancePrep mocks I pulled, what the MPhil layer actually tests, and the topics that aren't in your notes yet · Built 2026-05-26 The short version. The PEP site is a decent supplementary drill for the MPhil-specific layer (ethics, professional regulation, MSE, trauma therapy) that NET-style material skips. It is not a clean answer key, so treat its themes as a checklist, not gospel. I went through all 40 MPhil-specific questions across the two mocks, mapped them to your notes, and found 8 clusters you have zero or thin coverage on . Those are filled in below, exam-ready. 1. Verdict on PsychEntrancePrep (the site I pulled the mocks from) What it actually is A Google Sites page hosting mock tests as Google Forms and notes as Google Drive PDFs . The 120-question mocks split into 80 common (NET + MPhil) + 20 MPhil-specific + 20 UGC-NET-specific . I extracted both mocks' questions straight from the form data, but the forms are ungraded surveys with no official answer key — every correct answer and explanation on our quiz pages was authored by me with reasoning, not lifted from the site. Where it's good. Genuinely India-flavoured MPhil content (RCI, Indian Acts, MSE, ethics codes) that you won't get from generic NET PDFs. Free till the 31st. Wide topical spread. The MPhil-specific 20 per mock is the most useful slice for you because it targets the clinical-psych entrance layer specifically. Where to be careful. (1) No real answer key — a handful of items have defensible alternative answers, so if an explanation feels wrong, trust your reasoning and flag it. (2) Sloppy phrasing — stray "Q)" prefixes, typos, occasionally two arguable options. (3) The actual study notes are login-gated Drive PDFs scoped to one Workspace account, so I could only map their titles, not rip the text. (4) It's a coaching aggregator, not a primary source — for anything load-bearing, your NIMHANS PYQs and standard texts win. How to use it. Run the two MPhil sections as a themes checklist. The point isn't the score, it's surfacing the topics below that NET-style prep never made you study. 2. What the MPhil side actually tests Across the 40 MPhil-specific questions (20 in each mock), the weighting is heavily toward the professional / ethical / legal scaffolding of clinical practice — the stuff that separates an MPhil Clinical entrance from a general psych exam. Breakdown: 11 Ethics & professional 8 MSE & clinical assessment 6 Diagnosis & classification 6 Trauma / therapy modalities 5 LGBTQ / culture / minority 4 History & legal framework Question style is roughly half straight definitional recall ("who coined X", "what is Y") and half short applied vignette ("which principle is violated", "what is the correct sequence"). Difficulty is moderate — no trick stats, no deep neuroscience, but it assumes you've read the professional-practice and ethics chapters that NET prep tends to skip. 3. PKU = autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) . The enzyme normally converts phenylalanine → tyrosine . With PAH gone, phenylalanine piles up (toxic to brain in infancy) and tyrosine drops. The downstream consequence is intellectual disability, fair skin / hair (tyrosine is the precursor for melanin), and a musty body odour. Newborn screen catches it; treatment is a low-Phe diet for life. Section weighting from PYQs (rolling 3-year average) Section ~Q count / 100 Notes Therapy / Behaviour change ~19 Heaviest section. Reinforcement, conditioning, schools of therapy. Tier 2 — Asked twice across the three years T2 Study designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional, RCT) — pick best design for given scenario (rare outcome → case-control; rare exposure → cohort). T2 Validity types: face, content, construct (convergent + discriminant), criterion (concurrent + predictive). Tier 3 — Asked once each, recognise + classify T3 Levels of measurement (Stevens: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio). T3 Z-score interpretation; normal distribution properties (mean=median=mode, AUC=1, kurtosis types: leptokurtic / platykurtic / mesokurtic). T3 df for chi-square (rows−1)(cols−1). T3 Multicollinearity in regression; ANCOVA covariate assumption (linear with DV). T3 Partial correlation, biserial correlation, Spearman rank correlation. T3 Factorial ANOVA for interaction effects. text: This page is now split into four category sweeps. Sihan's call: don't add concepts one at a time, sweep the whole question type. Every named one is now organised by bucket — Effects , Phenomena , Theories , Theorists . This originators page stays the focused "who gave what" seed, with the three your prof flagged up top. Originators — "name the thing + who gave it" The "who proposed what" layer NIMHANS bolts on top of the clinical stuff. Named effects, complexes, personality concepts, social-psych theories, motivation theories and psychometrics terms, each pinned to the person who coined it. Built 2026-05-24 after your prof flagged Icarus complex, McCall's T and reactance as the kind of curveball they ask. Why this page exists. Your professor said the exam asked: the Icarus complex and who gave it, McCall's T , and reactance . None are core clinical. Two tells, not one: "who coined this named effect / complex / concept" (Icarus, McCall's T), AND "here's a phenomenon described in words, name the term" (reactance was this kind: the scenario was described and reactance was the answer). So learn the pairing and be able to recognise the concept from a plain-language description. The three he named are at the top, in the red box, first. Jump to: 0. The three he flagged 1. Named effects & complexes 1b. More complexes & syndromes 2. Personality theorists 3. Social psychology 3b. Influence & freedom (reactance) 4. Motivation & emotion 5. Psychometrics & measurement 5b. Statistical tests & who gave them (Student's t) 6. The standard-score family 0. The three your prof named Lock these cold. Term Who What it is Icarus complex Henry Murray A personality pattern of soaring ambition + craving for attention/admiration that ends in a fall (fascination with fire, ascent, falling, narcissism). Same Murray who gave the TAT , needs/press theory and personology . McCall's T score William McCall A standardised score with mean 50, SD 10 (no negatives, no decimals; MMPI uses it). Psychometrics, not clinical. Recognise it from the definition (that's how your prof asked it, not "who gave it"): they describe the score and the options are McCall's T vs other "t" things (Student's t, t-test, T-data). The trap is the shared letter: McCall's T = a standard score ; Student's t = a test statistic (Gosset) . Score with mean 50, SD 10 → McCall's T. (Psychological) reactance Jack Brehm (1966) The motivational push-back when you feel a freedom is being threatened or removed: you want the forbidden thing more . Social psych / motivation. Recognise it from a scenario (that's how your prof asked it): "told you can't have X, you now want X more / do it anyway" → reactance. "Reverse psychology" and the forbidden-fruit effect are reactance in action. Pattern to take away: personality theorists and their named complexes, social-psych theories with their author, and test/measurement jargon with the mean+SD. Everything below is that same layer, widened. 1. Named effects & complexes The classic "____ effect / ____ complex, who gave it" format. If a question names an effect, it usually wants the author. Effect / complex Originator What it is Jonah complex Abraham Maslow Fear of your own greatness; avoiding self-actualisation. (Opposite flavour to Icarus.) Inferiority / superiority complex Alfred Adler Core of Adlerian theory; overcompensation for felt inferiority. Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik We remember interrupted / incomplete tasks better than completed ones. Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (looks) bleeds into global positive judgement. (Reverse = horns effect .) Barnum / Forer effect Bertram Forer Accepting vague, general personality descriptions as uniquely true of you (horoscopes). Pygmalion effect Rosenthal & Jacobson Teacher's high expectations → student performs better. (Self-fulfilling prophecy in class.) Low expectation → Golem effect . Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric studies) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed . Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Liking something more simply from repeated exposure. Garcia effect (taste aversion) John Garcia One-trial conditioned aversion to a taste; biological preparedness; defies classic CC rules. Flynn effect James Flynn Population IQ scores have risen generation on generation. Matthew effect Robert Merton "Rich get richer" — early advantage compounds (used in reading/education). Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when it spells a conflicting colour word (attention/interference). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention: tuning one voice out of many, but still catching your name. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list is remembered best. Bystander effect Latané & Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Dunning–Kruger effect Dunning & Kruger Low-skill people overestimate their competence. Werther effect David Phillips Spike in copycat suicides after a publicised one. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Nisbett Paying someone for what they already enjoyed kills the intrinsic motivation . Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views/choices. Boomerang effect Hovland-era; akin to Brehm Persuasion backfires and pushes the attitude the opposite way. The cousin of reactance (§4). 1b. More named complexes & syndromes (Icarus, widened) Icarus complex was the curveball.
