text: Personality — the full book, chapter by chapter Not a summary. This is your Schultz & Schultz, Theories of Personality walked through in the book's own order, one chapter per theorist, with the book's signature recurring frame kept intact for each: the life (how the theorist's own biography shaped the theory), the theory unpacked in full, the book's Questions About Human Nature scorecard, Assessment , Research , and Reflections (the criticisms). After the book's chapters come the four domains the book underweights but NIMHANS tests hard, flagged in purple: object relations & self · existential · type theories · Indian / Triguna · assessment in depth . Built 2026-05-22 · Rewritten as a teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Poured out to full-book, chapter-by-chapter depth 2026-05-24 . Expanded to full depth 2026-05-24 (added the key studies walked through, an extended concept bank, an A–Z glossary, and a by-chapter self-test). How to read this page. Read it like the textbook, top to bottom, once; then revise off the coloured boxes. Each chapter follows the book: amber = the intuition / why it matters, amber "Human nature" = where the theorist lands on the book's six recurring issues. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-specific (clinical / Indian / rival-theory swaps). Grey recap = the chapter in one breath. The one-line testable list lives in Rapid Recall ; the personality tests in depth (MMPI/16PF/NEO/projectives, scoring) are on the tests deep-dive . Jump to: 1. What personality theory is 2. Freud 3. Jung 4. Adler 5. Horney 6. Erikson 7. Allport 8. Maslow 9. Rogers 10. Kelly 11. Skinner 12. Bandura 13. The trait approach & Five-Factor Model 14. Facets of personality 15. Personality in perspective S1. Object relations & self S2. The other neo-Freudians S3. Existential S4. Type theories S5. Indian psychology / Triguna S6. Assessment in depth At-a-glance compare All the MCQ traps Key studies, walked through Extended concept bank Fast glossary (A–Z) Self-test (active recall) The one frame that organises the whole book. The book ends every chapter by scoring the theorist on six recurring Questions About Human Nature . Hold these six and you can predict any theorist's "view of the person" answer: (1) free will vs determinism · (2) nature vs nurture (heredity vs environment) · (3) past vs present (does childhood fix us, or does the here-and-now/future drive us) · (4) uniqueness vs universality · (5) equilibrium vs growth (is the basic motive to reduce tension and stay balanced, or to grow ) · (6) optimism vs pessimism . Freud is the dark end of all six; the humanists are the bright end. Everyone else sits between. Part One · The study of personality Ch 1. Personality: what it is, and how the book studies it Personality is the relatively enduring, distinctive pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that characterises a person and how they adapt to the world. The word comes from the Latin persona , the mask the Roman actor wore, which already hides the book's central tension: is personality the mask we show, or the real face behind it? Every theory in the book is one answer to four questions: what is personality made of , where does it come from , why do people differ , and can it change . The book groups the theorists into approaches , and that grouping is the spine of the table of contents: the psychoanalytic (Freud); the neopsychoanalytic (Jung, Adler, Horney); the life-span (Erikson); the genetics/trait pioneer (Allport); the humanistic (Maslow, Rogers); the cognitive (Kelly); the behavioural (Skinner); the social-learning (Bandura); the trait approach (Cattell, Eysenck, the Five-Factor Model); and the facet / limited-domain theories (Rotter, Zuckerman, Seligman). How the book assesses and researches personality The book insists every theory must answer two practical questions, and the recurring "Assessment" and "Research" sections grade each theorist on them: Assessment = how do you measure this theory's constructs? The methods recur: self-report inventories (objective, scored against norms, e.g. MMPI, 16PF, NEO), projective techniques (ambiguous stimuli, e.g. Rorschach, TAT), clinical interviews , behavioural assessment , and idiographic personal documents (diaries, letters). A good test must clear three bars: reliability (consistency), validity (measures what it claims), and standardised norms . Research = how was the theory tested ? Three designs recur: the clinical method (case studies, the dominant psychoanalytic tool, rich but unreliable and unrepresentative), the experimental method (manipulate a variable, the only route to cause and effect), and the correlational method (relate two measured variables, covariation only, never causation). TRAP — method by camp. Case study / clinical method = the psychoanalysts (Freud, Jung, Adler). Correlational + factor analysis = the trait theorists (Cattell, Eysenck, FFM). Controlled experiment = the behaviourists and social-learning theorists (Skinner, Bandura) and Rogers, who pioneered experimental psychotherapy research. The method usually tells you the camp. Recap Ch 1. Personality = the enduring, distinctive pattern of how a person thinks, feels and behaves. The book is organised by approach and grades every theorist on six human-nature issues plus Assessment and Research. Nomothetic (general laws, trait research) vs idiographic (the unique individual, case studies) is the master methodological split. Part Two · The psychoanalytic approach Ch 2. Sigmund Freud — psychoanalysis The life (1856–1939). Born in Moravia, raised in Vienna, the adored eldest son of a young mother (the book notes this shaped his Oedipal theory). Trained as a neurologist; studied hysteria under Charcot in Paris and worked with Josef Breuer , whose patient Anna O. coined the "talking cure". A flirtation with cocaine, a long self-analysis after his father's death (the engine of The Interpretation of Dreams , 1900), decades of jaw cancer, and finall

title: Phenomena — illusions, biases, attention/memory glitches & neuropsych signs
text: Phenomena — illusions, biases, attention/memory glitches & neuropsych signs Second of the four category sweeps. The bucket is "named phenomena": things the mind/brain does that get a name. Perceptual illusions, attention failures, memory phenomena, group phenomena, cognitive biases and neuropsych signs. The stem usually describes the experience and wants the name (or who described it). Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes Effect vs phenomenon — same idea, different label. If the term ends in "effect" it's on the Effects page; if it's described as a phenomenon, bias, illusion or sign, it's here. NIMHANS picks whichever label fits the stem, so scan both. Jump to: 1. Perceptual illusions 2. Gestalt grouping 3. Attention & perception 4. Memory phenomena 5. Group / social 6. Cognitive biases 7. Neuropsych & clinical signs 1. Perceptual illusions Illusion Who What you see Müller-Lyer Franz Müller-Lyer Two equal lines look unequal depending on arrow-head direction (inward vs outward fins). Ponzo Mario Ponzo Two equal lines on converging "railway" lines look unequal (depth misread). Ebbinghaus (Titchener) circles Ebbinghaus A circle ringed by big circles looks smaller than the same circle ringed by small ones. Zöllner Zöllner Parallel lines look slanted because of crossing hatch marks. Kanizsa triangle Gaetano Kanizsa You "see" a white triangle edge that isn't drawn (illusory/subjective contours). Necker cube Louis Necker A wire cube flips between two 3-D orientations (bistable perception). Rubin's vase Edgar Rubin Faces-or-vase: figure–ground reversal. Ames room Adelbert Ames A distorted room makes equal-size people look giant vs tiny. Moon illusion — The moon looks larger near the horizon than overhead. Hermann grid — Ghostly grey blobs appear at the white intersections of a black grid. Café wall Gregory & Heard Straight mortar lines look wedge-shaped between offset tiles. Phi phenomenon Max Wertheimer Lights flashing in sequence look like one moving light (the founding Gestalt demo of apparent motion). Autokinetic phenomenon used by Sherif A still point of light in the dark seems to drift; Sherif used it to study norm formation. Two "size of equal lines" illusions: Müller-Lyer = arrow fins; Ponzo = converging rails. Ebbinghaus = circles surrounded by other circles. Examiners mix these three. 2. Gestalt grouping principles Wertheimer, Koffka & Köhler. "The whole is other than the sum of its parts." Master law = Prägnanz (we see the simplest, most stable form). Principle What groups together Proximity Things close together are seen as a group. Similarity Things that look alike are grouped. Continuity (good continuation) We follow smooth, continuous lines over abrupt changes. Closure We fill gaps to see a complete figure. Figure–ground We split a scene into an object and its background. Common fate Things moving together are grouped. Prägnanz (good form) The overarching law: perceive the simplest, most regular organisation. 3. Attention & perception phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Inattentional blindness Mack & Rock; Simons & Chabris (gorilla) You miss an obvious unexpected object while attending elsewhere. Change blindness Simons & Levin You fail to notice a large change across a visual interruption. Attentional blink Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell Brief inability to detect a 2nd target ~200–500 ms after the 1st. Cocktail-party phenomenon Colin Cherry Tracking one voice in noise, yet still catching your own name. Weber's law / JND Ernst Weber The just-noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the stimulus. Fechner's law Gustav Fechner Sensation grows with the log of stimulus intensity (founded psychophysics). Sensory adaptation — Constant stimulation → declining response (you stop feeling your clothes). Pareidolia — Seeing meaningful patterns (faces) in random stimuli (clouds, toast). Synaesthesia — One sense automatically triggers another (hearing colours, tasting words). Blindsight Weiskrantz Responding to visual stimuli without conscious sight (V1 damage). Perceptual constancy — Objects seen as stable in size/shape/colour despite changing retinal image. 4. Memory phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) Brown & McNeill Knowing a word is there but not retrieving it (you often get its first letter/length). Flashbulb memory Brown & Kulik Vivid, confident memory of where you were during a shocking event (often inaccurate). Déjà vu / jamais vu — Novel scene feels familiar / familiar scene feels alien. Reminiscence bump — Older adults recall disproportionately many memories from ages ~10–30. Childhood (infantile) amnesia — Few/no episodic memories before ~age 3–4. Proactive interference — Old learning blocks new (old password keeps coming up). Retroactive interference — New learning blocks old (new password erases the old one). Forgetting curve Hermann Ebbinghaus Retention drops sharply then levels off; relearning is faster (savings). Misattribution / source monitoring error Schacter Right memory, wrong source (cryptomnesia: feeling you invented something you read). 5. Group & social phenomena Phenomenon Who What it is Social facilitation Triplett; Zajonc Presence of others boosts easy tasks, harms hard ones. Social loafing Latané; Ringelmann roots Individuals slack in groups when effort isn't identifiable. Diffusion of responsibility Darley & Latané The mechanism behind the bystander effect: "someone else will." Group polarisation Moscovici; Stoner (risky shift) Group discussion pushes members to a more extreme version of their leaning. Groupthink Irving Janis Cohesive group suppresses dissent for consensus → bad decisions. Deindividuation Festinger; Zimbardo Loss of self-awareness/restraint in a crowd or anonymity. Conformity Solomon Asch Going along with a group's wrong judgement (line task). Obedience Stanley Milgram Following authority's orders against your own conscience (shock study). Bystander apathy Latané & Dar

title: Personality & Projective Tests, Deep Reference
text: Personality & Projective Tests, Deep Reference Built 2026-05-19 after you flagged that the test entries on the assessment cheatsheet were too thin. This page does one job: for every personality + projective + Beck/Bell inventory in the MET/NIMHANS pool, give you item count, scales/subscales, scoring, author + year, and use case in one screen. Memorize the numbers in bold, the rest is texture. Cross-link with the read-first primer for reliability/validity and the revision pack for the one-page table. How MCQ-writers attack this section. Almost every question is one of four moves: (1) swap the item count between two tests, (2) swap the author or year, (3) ask which scale belongs to which test, (4) ask which test is projective vs objective. So your job here is to lock the quadruple (test → items → scales → author/year) cold. Get those four right and you bank the marks. 1. MMPI Family (Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory) MMPI (original, 1943) Authors: Starke R. Hathaway (psychologist) & J. Charnley McKinley (psychiatrist), University of Minnesota. Year: 1943. Items: 566 true/false statements (often reported as 550 unique + 16 repeats; the canonical number you quote is 566 ). Method of construction: empirical criterion-keyed. Items were retained only if they discriminated a diagnostic group from normals — not based on face validity. This was the breakthrough method versus older content-based inventories. Original norming sample: "Minnesota normals" (724 visitors to the Univ. of Minnesota Hospitals) — later criticised as a narrow, mostly white rural Midwest base, which drove the MMPI-2 restandardisation. MMPI-2 (the version exam-writers mean by default) Year: 1989 (restandardisation), revised manual 2001. Items: 567 true/false items. Memorize this exact number. Age range: 18+ years. Reading level: 6th grade. Administration time: 60–90 minutes. Scoring: scores converted to T-scores (mean 50, SD 10). Clinically significant elevation: T ≥ 65 on MMPI-2 (was T ≥ 70 on original MMPI). 10 clinical scales (memorize the order, scale 5 and 0 are the supplementary ones): # Code Name What it picks up 1 Hs Hypochondriasis Bodily preoccupation, somatic complaints 2 D Depression Sadness, hopelessness, low morale 3 Hy Hysteria Conversion features, somatic + denial 4 Pd Psychopathic Deviate Authority conflict, antisocial features 5 Mf Masculinity-Femininity Gender-role interest pattern 6 Pa Paranoia Suspiciousness, ideas of reference 7 Pt Psychasthenia Anxiety, obsessional rumination, doubt 8 Sc Schizophrenia Bizarre thought, alienation 9 Ma Hypomania Elevated mood, overactivity, grandiosity 0 Si Social Introversion Social withdrawal vs sociability Validity scales (the L/F/K triad is the high-yield bit): ? (Cannot Say): number of unanswered items. > 30 omissions invalidates profile. L (Lie): 15 items detecting naive "faking good" — claiming impossibly virtuous behaviour ("I have never told a lie"). High L = unsophisticated impression management. F (Infrequency): 60 items rarely endorsed by normals. High F = random responding, malingering, or genuine severe pathology. Cannot distinguish those without further evidence. K (Correction): 30 items measuring subtle defensiveness. Used as a correction factor added to 5 clinical scales (1, 4, 7, 8, 9) to compensate for guardedness. VRIN (Variable Response Inconsistency): inconsistent answers to similar items → random responding. TRIN (True Response Inconsistency): all-true or all-false bias. F B (Back F): infrequency on later items, catches fatigue or "give-up" responding. F p (F-Psychopathology): infrequency among psychiatric inpatients; helps separate malingering from genuine pathology. Interpretation logic. Profile is plotted with all scales on one graph in T-score units. Clinicians read code types (e.g., "2-7/7-2" = elevations on Depression + Psychasthenia → classic anxious-depressed picture; "4-9" = antisocial acting-out). Single-scale interpretation is discouraged. MMPI-2-RF (Restructured Form, 2008) Items: 338. Scales: 9 Restructured Clinical (RC) scales + a demoralization scale (RCd) + higher-order scales. The "common variance" of demoralization is pulled out so each RC scale measures something more specific. Use: shorter, psychometrically tighter version. Increasingly the research default but MET still tests the classic MMPI-2 numbers. MMPI-3 (2020) Items: 335. New norms. Scales: 52 total — H-O scales, RC scales, Specific Problem (SP) scales, PSY-5 scales. MMPI-A (Adolescent) Items: 478. Ages 14–18. Released 1992. There is also an MMPI-A-RF (2016, 241 items). 2. 16PF (Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire) Author: Raymond B. Cattell (with Tatsuoka & Eber on later editions). Year: first edition 1949. Current edition is the 16PF Fifth Edition (1993) . Items: 185 items (5th edition). Each item is 3-choice: agree / ? / disagree, except the reasoning subtest which is forced-choice. Age range: 16+ years. Administration time: 35–50 minutes. Method of construction: factor analysis of the lexicon. Cattell started with Allport & Odbert's list of ~4500 trait words, reduced to ~160 surface traits, then factor-analysed to 16 source traits . Scoring: raw scores → Sten scores (Standard Ten: mean 5.5, SD 2, range 1–10). Sten 1–3 = low pole, 4–7 = average, 8–10 = high pole. The 16 primary factors (Cattell letter codes; you do not have to memorize every letter but the names of the high/low poles get tested): Code Low pole ←→ High pole A Reserved ↔ Warm B Concrete reasoning ↔ Abstract reasoning C Reactive (emotional) ↔ Emotionally stable E Deferential ↔ Dominant F Serious ↔ Lively G Expedient ↔ Rule-conscious H Shy ↔ Socially bold I Utilitarian ↔ Sensitive L Trusting ↔ Vigilant M Grounded ↔ Abstracted N Forthright ↔ Private O Self-assured ↔ Apprehensive Q1 Traditional ↔ Open to change Q2 Group-oriented ↔ Self-reliant Q3 Tolerates disorder ↔ Perfectionistic Q4 Relaxed ↔ Tense 5 global factors (second-order, conceptually close to the Big Five): Extraversion, Anxiety, T

text: Psychotherapy, Full Section Cheatsheet Section 5 of MET. 15 questions (MET) / 10 (NIMHANS). Built 2026-05-17 to close the cheatsheet gap noted on the notes index. School-by-school. Founders, mechanism, technique, indication, MCQ trap. Cross-link with the Learning & Conditioning page for behaviour-therapy terms and the consolidated revision pack for Ellis vs Beck, defenses, and CBT triggers. 1. Psychoanalytic / Psychodynamic Freud, the scaffolding Topographic model: conscious, preconscious, unconscious. Structural model: id (pleasure principle, primary process), ego (reality principle, secondary process), superego (conscience + ego ideal). Psychosexual stages: oral (0-1.5), anal (1.5-3), phallic (3-6) — Oedipus / Electra, latency (6-puberty), genital (puberty-adulthood). Fixation → adult character traits. Defenses: Vaillant hierarchy: psychotic (denial, distortion) → immature (projection, acting out, regression, somatization) → neurotic (intellectualisation, displacement, reaction formation, repression, isolation of affect) → mature (humour, sublimation, suppression, altruism, anticipation). Classical technique Free association — the fundamental rule. Interpretation of resistances and transference. Dream analysis — manifest vs latent content. Working through — repeated re-examination across contexts until insight becomes integrated and behavioural change emerges. Distinguishes intellectual from emotional/behavioural insight. Frequency: classical psychoanalysis 3-5×/week, couch, years. Psychoanalytic / psychodynamic therapy: 1-2×/week, face-to-face, months-years. Post-Freudians, the canon Theorist Core contribution Alfred Adler Individual Psychology. Inferiority feelings → striving for superiority. Social interest. Birth order. Style of life. Early recollections in assessment. Carl Jung Analytical Psychology. Collective unconscious. Archetypes (persona, shadow, anima/animus, self). Individuation. Introversion/extraversion. Word association test. Anna Freud Ego psychology. Defense mechanisms systematised. Child analysis through play. Melanie Klein Object relations. Paranoid-schizoid → depressive position. Splitting, projective identification. Internal objects. Play therapy. Donald Winnicott Object relations. "Good-enough mother," holding environment, true vs false self, transitional object. Heinz Kohut Self psychology. Narcissistic injury, mirroring, idealising, twinship selfobjects. Empathic immersion. Karen Horney Basic anxiety. Neurotic needs. "Tyranny of the should." Feminine psychology critique of Freud. Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages (Trust v Mistrust → Integrity v Despair). Identity crisis. Ego psychology bridge to lifespan dev. Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal psychiatry. "Self-system." Anxiety as interpersonal. Influenced IPT. Otto Kernberg Transference-Focused Psychotherapy (TFP) for BPD. Borderline personality organisation. Splitting + identity diffusion. MCQ trap: Working through is NOT free association nor a single interpretation; it is repeated re-encounter with the same conflict/insight in shifting contexts until consolidated. Common distractor in MET / NIMHANS. 2. Behaviour Therapy Founders: Joseph Wolpe , Hans Eysenck , B. F. Skinner , Albert Bandura . Mechanism: directly manipulate antecedents, behaviours, consequences via classical + operant conditioning + social learning. Core techniques Technique Mechanism Indication Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) Reciprocal inhibition: relaxation paired with graded imagined exposure up a fear hierarchy Phobias (classic) In-vivo exposure Real-world graded exposure without relaxation; habituation + extinction Specific phobia, agoraphobia, OCD, PTSD Flooding / implosion Full-intensity exposure without escape until anxiety extinguishes Phobias (less used due to dropout) Exposure & Response Prevention (ERP) (Foa, Kozak) Exposure to obsessional trigger + prevention of compulsive response OCD — first-line behavioural Tx Aversion therapy Pairing unwanted behaviour with aversive UCS (covert sensitisation as imaginal version) Paraphilias, substance use (limited evidence + ethical issues) Token economy Operant: secondary reinforcers (tokens) exchanged for primary reinforcers Inpatient / institutional settings, ID, ADHD classrooms Contingency management Operant: rewards contingent on target behaviour SUDs (esp. stimulant) Behavioural activation (Lewinsohn, Jacobson) Scheduled engagement in rewarding/mastery activities; reverses depressive withdrawal-rumination cycle Depression — comparable to CBT Modeling (Bandura) Observational learning, vicarious reinforcement; participant modeling Phobias, social skills Shaping Reinforce successive approximations of target behaviour Skill acquisition, autism intervention Chaining Link sequential behaviours into a longer behavioural chain (forward or backward chaining) ADL skills training Biofeedback Real-time physiological readouts (EMG, HRV, GSR, EEG) shape autonomic / muscle control Tension headache, migraine, anxiety, urinary incontinence Full primer on behaviour-therapy terms: Learning & Conditioning (priming, shaping, chaining, fading, prompting, all 4 reinforcement schedules, extinction, generalisation, latent/insight/observational learning, habituation vs sensitisation). MCQ trap: ERP is the first-line behavioural treatment for OCD (SSRIs first-line pharmacotherapy). Systematic desensitisation is for phobias, not OCD. 3. Cognitive and Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy Beck's Cognitive Therapy Cognitive triad of depression: negative views of (1) self, (2) world/experience, (3) future. Schemas → automatic thoughts → emotion/behaviour. Common cognitive distortions: all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralisation, mental filter, disqualifying the positive, jumping to conclusions (mind reading / fortune telling), magnification or minimisation, emotional reasoning, "should" statements, labelling, personalisation. Techniques: Socratic questioning (guided discovery), thought records, downward arrow, behavioura

title: Research Methodology & Statistics — learn it cold
text: Research Methodology & Statistics — learn it cold Built from A. K. Singh, Tests, Measurements and Research Methods in Behavioural Sciences (the Indian standard, strong on measurement, test construction and item analysis) paired with Coolican, Research Methods and Statistics in Psychology (clear on design, logic of inference and which test to run). Don't memorise tables blind — read the prose, understand why each statistic does what it does, then the tables are just reminders. Formulas are given in plain text where one exists. Trap boxes flag the exact confusions MCQs are built to exploit; NIMHANS boxes flag where the clinical-psych entrance pushes deeper than MET. 1 Measurement 2 Descriptive 3 Distributions 4 Inferential logic 5 Parametric tests 6 Non-parametric 7 Correlation & regression 8 Reliability & validity 9 Sampling 10 Designs 11 Variables 12 Study validity 13 Qualitative 14 Item analysis 15 Ethics 16 Scaling Decision table MCQ traps Worked intuition Glossary Self-test 1. Levels of Measurement Before any statistic, ask: what kind of numbers am I holding? Stevens (1946) showed that a number can carry four different amounts of information, and the amount of information you have dictates which statistics are even meaningful . Running a mean on jersey numbers is nonsense not because the arithmetic fails but because the numbers were never on a scale where "average" means anything. This is the single most important idea in the whole section: the scale chooses the test. The four levels, from least to most information (NOIR) Nominal — labels only Numbers are just names for categories with no order: 1 = male, 2 = female, or blood groups, religion, diagnosis. You can count how many fall in each box and find the mode (most frequent category), but "2 > 1" is meaningless. Permissible stats: frequencies, proportions, mode, and chi-square on the counts. Ordinal — rank order, unequal gaps Numbers now carry order but the distance between ranks is not equal or known. Finishing 1st, 2nd, 3rd tells you who beat whom, not by how much. Likert agreement, pain 0–10, socio-economic class. Because gaps are unequal you should not really add or average them, so the centre is the median and the spread is described with percentiles. Permissible: median, percentile, Spearman's rho , Mann-Whitney U , and rank-based (non-parametric) tests generally. Interval — equal gaps, no true zero Equal distances mean a degree is a degree everywhere on the scale, so you can finally add, subtract, and take a mean . But zero is arbitrary (0°C is not "no temperature"), so ratios are meaningless : 20°C is not "twice as hot" as 10°C. IQ and calendar years sit here. Permissible: mean, SD, t-tests, ANOVA, Pearson's r . Ratio — equal gaps and an absolute zero Zero means none of the thing (0 kg = no weight, 0 ms reaction time = no time). Now ratios are valid : 40 kg really is twice 20 kg. Height, weight, reaction time, income, age. All arithmetic plus the geometric mean. For test-choice purposes interval and ratio behave identically, which is why people lump them as "scale" or "continuous" data. Level Property added Example Centre Permissible stats Nominal Categories, no order Sex, blood group, diagnosis Mode Frequency, proportion, chi-square Ordinal + Order (unequal gaps) Likert, pain 0–10, SES class Median Median, percentile, Spearman, Mann-Whitney Interval + Equal gaps (no true 0) °C, IQ, calendar year Mean Mean, SD, t, ANOVA, Pearson r Ratio + True zero (ratios valid) Height, weight, RT, age Mean All of the above + geometric mean, CV Memory hook: NOIR — Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio, in increasing order of information. They swap these: a scale "having numbers" does not make it interval. A 1–5 Likert item is strictly ordinal (the gap from "disagree" to "neutral" need not equal "neutral" to "agree"); only a summed multi-item Likert scale is commonly treated as interval. MCQs love "temperature in Celsius is ratio" — false, no true zero; Kelvin is ratio. They swap these: "ordinal data can use the mean." It has no defensible mean because the gaps are unequal — use the median. Recap. Four levels, NOIR. Nominal = labels (mode, chi-square). Ordinal = ranks (median, rank tests). Interval = equal gaps, arbitrary zero (mean, parametric tests, but no ratios). Ratio = true zero (everything). The level you have is the gatekeeper for every test that follows. 2. Descriptive Statistics Descriptive statistics summarise the sample in front of you ; they make no claim about a wider population (that's inference, section 4). You describe three things about any batch of numbers: where the centre sits ( central tendency ), how spread out it is ( dispersion ), and what shape it has ( skewness, kurtosis ). Central tendency — where the middle is Mean The arithmetic average: add all scores, divide by n. In symbols x̄ = Σx / n . It uses every value, which is its strength and its weakness — every value includes the outliers. One billionaire walking into a room sends the mean income soaring while the median barely moves. Use the mean for roughly symmetric / normal interval-ratio data. Median The middle value when scores are ordered (the 50th percentile). With an even n it's the average of the two middle scores. It ignores the actual magnitude of extreme scores, so it is robust to outliers and skew . Use it for skewed data (income, reaction times, length of hospital stay) and for ordinal data. Mode The most frequent value. It's the only central-tendency measure usable on nominal data, and a distribution can be bimodal or multimodal (two humps often hints two subgroups are mixed together). Why skew moves them apart: in a symmetric distribution mean = median = mode. In a positive (right) skew (long tail of high values, e.g. income) the tail drags the mean up the most, the median less, the mode least, so mode < median < mean . In a negative (left) skew it reverses: mean < median < mode . The mean always chases the tail. Hook: the mean follows the tail. They sw

title: Sleep, Full Primer
text: Sleep, Full Primer Sleep, Full Primer Built 2026-04-22 after Sihan reported “I do not know anything about sleep.” This covers everything MET might ask, organized from macro (architecture) to micro (neurochemistry) to clinical (disorders). Memorize the tables. 1. Macro View: Sleep is Two Modes Sleep splits into NREM (Non-REM) and REM (Rapid Eye Movement) . NREM has 3 stages. Total = 4 stages of sleep. NREM REM Brain activity Slows progressively Fast, almost like awake Muscle tone Normal, relaxed Atonia (paralyzed) Eye movements Slow or absent Rapid bursts Dreaming Rare, thought-like Vivid, narrative Heart rate / BP Low, stable Variable, elevated Breathing Slow, regular Irregular Thermoregulation Works Fails (we do not shiver/sweat normally) Memory role Declarative consolidation (esp. NREM 3) Procedural + emotional consolidation 2. The Four Stages NREM Stage 1 — Transition (about 5% of night) EEG: theta waves (4–8 Hz) . Very light sleep, easily woken. People often say they were not asleep. Hypnagogic images, muscle twitches (hypnic jerks). Duration: 5–10 minutes at start of night. NREM Stage 2 — Light Sleep (about 45–55% of night) EEG: theta + sleep spindles (12–14 Hz bursts) + K-complexes (large single waves). Core sign of being “truly asleep.” Body temperature drops, heart rate slows. Most of the night spent here. Increases as night progresses. Spindles come from the thalamus, gate sensory input so you stay asleep. NREM Stage 3 — Slow-Wave Sleep / Deep Sleep / Delta (about 15–20%) EEG: delta waves (0.5–4 Hz), high amplitude . Deepest sleep. Hard to rouse. If woken, groggy (sleep inertia). Growth hormone released here. Immune repair, glycogen restoration. Parasomnias (sleepwalking, sleep terrors, bedwetting) come OUT of NREM 3, not REM. Common in children because children have more delta sleep. Dominates the FIRST HALF of the night. REM — Paradoxical Sleep (about 20–25%) EEG: mixed frequency, low amplitude , looks almost like awake. “Paradoxical” because brain is active but body is paralyzed. Muscle atonia (pons actively suppresses motor output via medial medulla → spinal cord). Only eye muscles and diaphragm keep moving. Vivid narrative dreams. Emotional, story-like. Eye bursts (the “RE” in REM). Autonomic instability: irregular HR, BP, breathing. Penile/clitoral tumescence. REM episodes GET LONGER across the night. First REM is short (10 min), last REM can be 45+ min. Dominates the SECOND HALF of the night. 3. Sleep Cycle Architecture One full cycle = ~90 minutes . Sequence through the night, typical young adult: Night start: Wake → N1 → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM → (first cycle, ~90 min, mostly N3, short REM) → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM → (second cycle, less N3, longer REM) → N2 → REM → (third cycle, minimal N3, long REM) → N2 → REM → (fourth / fifth cycles: REM-dominated, minimal N3) 4–6 cycles per 8 hours. First half of night = deep sleep heavy (N3 for body repair). Second half = REM heavy (for memory consolidation and dreams). If sleep is cut short, you lose REM disproportionately. 4. Neural Control Sleep onset Promoted by adenosine accumulating through the day (caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, which is why coffee keeps you awake). VLPO (Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus) of the hypothalamus = “sleep switch.” GABAergic, inhibits wake-promoting regions. Melatonin from pineal gland, released in darkness. Wake Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) of the brainstem. Neurotransmitters: histamine (tuberomammillary nucleus), orexin/hypocretin (lateral hypothalamus), norepinephrine (locus coeruleus), serotonin (raphe), acetylcholine (PPT/LDT). Loss of orexin neurons = narcolepsy . REM vs NREM switching Driven by a flip-flop between: REM-ON cells: cholinergic neurons in PPT/LDT (acetylcholine surge during REM). REM-OFF cells: aminergic neurons (NE in locus coeruleus, 5-HT in raphe) — silent during REM. Atonia mechanism: during REM, pontine REM-on neurons activate medial medulla (magnocellular nucleus) → hyperpolarizes spinal motor neurons → full-body paralysis except diaphragm and eyes. Circadian SCN (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) of the hypothalamus = master clock, ~24.2 hr intrinsic period. Entrained by light via the retinohypothalamic tract (non-visual, from intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells). SCN → pineal gland → melatonin release in darkness. Core body temperature dips at night (~2 AM), rises in morning. 5. Sleep Across the Lifespan Age Total sleep % REM Notes Newborn 16–18 hrs ~50% Enters sleep via REM (adults enter via N1) Infant (1 yr) 14 hrs ~30% — Child (5 yr) 11–12 hrs ~25% Most parasomnias occur now Adolescent 9 hrs ~20% Delayed sleep phase is developmentally normal Adult 7–8 hrs ~20–25% Standard baseline Elderly (65+) 6–7 hrs ~15–20% Less N3, more awakenings, phase advance 6. Sleep Disorders (DSM-5, MCQ High Yield) Dyssomnias (difficulty with amount/timing/quality) Disorder Core feature Treatment Insomnia Difficulty falling/staying asleep, 3 nights/wk × 3 months CBT-I first line, then hypnotics short-term Narcolepsy Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden muscle tone loss triggered by emotion), sleep paralysis , hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations . Cause: orexin/hypocretin deficiency . REM intrudes into wake. Modafinil, stimulants; sodium oxybate for cataplexy Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) Airway collapses during sleep, repeated apneas/hypopneas, snoring, daytime sleepiness CPAP Central Sleep Apnea Brainstem fails to signal breathing CPAP/BiPAP Restless Legs Syndrome Urge to move legs, worse at rest/night, relieved by movement. Dopamine deficit, low iron Dopamine agonists (pramipexole), iron Circadian Rhythm Disorders Delayed sleep phase, advanced sleep phase, shift work, jet lag Light therapy, melatonin Kleine-Levin Syndrome Recurrent episodes of hypersomnia + hyperphagia + hypersexuality. Young males Rare Parasomnias (abnormal events during sleep) Disorder Stage Core feature Sleepwalking (somnambulism) NREM 3 Complex motor activity, eyes open, no memory. Child

title: Social Psychology: the full chapter, from scratch
text: Social Psychology: the full chapter, from scratch Read this like a textbook, not a cheatsheet. Every chapter explained from first principles, then the named effects, the theorists and the traps. Anchored to your Baron & Branscombe, Social Psychology (13th ed.) , walked through in book order: the science & its methods · social cognition · perception & attribution · the self · attitudes & persuasion · prejudice · attraction & love · social influence · prosocial behaviour · aggression · groups. NIMHANS weights this domain heavily (heavier than MET), and the dominant question type is which name goes with which effect , so the attribution-style pairs are flagged throughout. Built 2026-05-24 · Rewritten as a full teaching chapter 2026-05-24 · Deepened to full-book depth 2026-05-24 · Expanded to ~50 pages 2026-05-24 (added the landmark studies walked through step by step, an extended concept bank covering every remaining Baron term per chapter, and an A–Z fast glossary). Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use this page. It is built to learn from , not just revise. Each topic has: (1) the problem it was trying to solve, (2) the core idea in plain language with an everyday example, (3) the named concepts unpacked one by one in tables, and (4) coloured boxes recapping the exam-testable fact and the trap. Amber boxes = the intuition / why it matters. Green = the line to lock. Red = the MCQ trap. Purple = NIMHANS-specific (clinical / Indian context, rival-theory swaps). Grey recap = the section in one breath. The one-line testable list lives in Rapid Recall ; the four type sweeps are the chips above. Jump to: 0. Social psych as a science 1. Social cognition 2. Perception & attribution 3. The self 4. Attitudes & persuasion 5. Prejudice 6. Attraction & love 7. Social influence 8. Prosocial 9. Aggression 10. Groups 11. Landmark studies, walked through 12. Extended concept bank 13. MCQ traps, collected 14. Fast glossary 15. Self-test (active recall) 0. Social psychology as a science What the field actually claims. Social psychology is the scientific study of how the thoughts, feelings and behaviour of individuals are influenced by the actual, imagined or implied presence of others (Allport's classic definition). The key word is scientific : it does not settle questions by intuition or anecdote, it runs studies. And the key insight, repeated throughout Baron, is the power of the situation : ordinary people do extraordinary things (help, conform, obey, aggress) far more because of where they are and who is around than because of fixed traits. That theme, situation over disposition, returns in obedience (Milgram), bystander apathy (Latané & Darley) and the attribution chapter (the FAE is precisely our failure to see it). The role of theory. A theory is an integrated set of principles that explains and predicts observed events. Good social psychology runs a loop: a theory generates a specific, falsifiable hypothesis ; a study tests it; results refine or refute the theory. A theory is never "proven", only supported or disconfirmed, and it earns its keep by making predictions that could have failed but did not. The three core research methods Baron's methods chapter contrasts three ways to gather evidence, each with a trade-off between control and realism. Method What you do Strength / limit Experimental Manipulate one factor (the independent variable, IV ), hold everything else constant, measure the effect on the dependent variable, DV . Use random assignment to conditions. The only method that establishes cause and effect . Limit: artificiality, low external validity if over-controlled. Correlational Measure two or more variables as they naturally occur and see if they covary (correlation coefficient, −1 to +1). Good for real-world variables you cannot ethically manipulate. Limit: correlation ≠ causation (direction problem + third-variable problem). Survey Ask a representative sample questions to describe a population's attitudes/behaviour. Cheap, broad. Limit: sampling bias, wording effects, social-desirability responding. The IV/DV intuition. The IV is the cause you dial (the dose), the DV is the effect you read off (the symptom). Picture the experimenter's hand on a knob (IV) and an eye on a dial (DV). Random assignment is what lets you claim the knob, not some pre-existing difference between people, moved the dial. Correlational work has no knob, you only watch two dials move together, which is why it cannot tell you which one is driving. Mediators, moderators and meta-analysis A mediator is the mechanism , the variable that comes between cause and effect and explains why the IV affects the DV (frustration → anger → aggression: anger mediates). A moderator is a variable that changes the strength or direction of the relationship, telling you when or for whom it holds (heat increases aggression more for provoked people). A meta-analysis statistically combines many studies to estimate the true overall effect size, the gold standard for asking "does this effect really hold?" Deception, ethics and replication Because telling participants the true purpose would change their behaviour, social psychology often uses deception (a cover story). This is allowed only under strict ethical safeguards: informed consent , the right to withdraw, minimising harm, and a thorough debriefing afterwards that reveals the true purpose and removes any deception's after-effects. An Institutional Review Board / ethics committee must approve the study first. The discipline has also taken its replication crisis seriously: a finding is trusted only when independent labs replicate it, which is why classic single studies (Milgram, the marshmallow studies) are now discussed alongside their replications and failures. text: Theories — every named theory/model, its author, the one-line hook Third of the four category sweeps. The bucket is "named theories/models." Grouped by domain so you see the rival theories side by side (that's how they're tested: "which theory says X?" or "who proposed it?"). Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes Two question shapes. (1) "Who gave [theory]?" → name the author. (2) "Which theory holds that [claim]?" → name the theory. Rival theories in one domain are each other's distractors (James-Lange vs Cannon-Bard, Piaget vs Vygotsky), so always learn the contrast , not the theory alone. Jump to: 1. Learning 2. Motivation 3. Emotion 4. Personality 5. Development 6. Social 7. Intelligence 8. Memory & cognition 9. Language 10. Stress & abnormal 11. Perception 12. Career & counselling 1. Learning theories Theory Author Core claim Classical conditioning Ivan Pavlov Neutral stimulus paired with a reflex-evoking one comes to evoke the reflex. Connectionism / Law of Effect Edward Thorndike Responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in (trial-and-error, puzzle box). Operant conditioning B. F. Skinner Behaviour is shaped by its consequences (reinforcement/punishment). Contiguity theory Edwin Guthrie One-trial learning by sheer stimulus–response pairing in time. Insight learning Wolfgang Köhler Sudden restructuring of a problem ("aha"), shown in chimps (Sultan). Latent learning / cognitive maps Edward Tolman Learning happens without reinforcement and shows up later (maze rats). Social / observational learning Albert Bandura We learn by watching and modelling others (Bobo doll). Rescorla–Wagner model Rescorla & Wagner Conditioning depends on surprise / prediction error, not mere pairing. Premack principle David Premack A high-frequency activity can reinforce a low-frequency one ("grandma's rule"). Conditions / hierarchy of learning Robert Gagné Eight learning types from signal learning up to problem-solving; later five learned capabilities + nine instructional events. Meaningful learning / advance organizers David Ausubel New material is learned by anchoring it to existing knowledge; pre-teach an advance organizer first. Reception, not discovery. Discovery learning Jerome Bruner Learn by exploring and figuring it out yourself; spiral curriculum; enactive → iconic → symbolic representation. Two-factor (avoidance) theory O. H. Mowrer Avoidance learning = classical conditioning of fear + operant reinforcement from escaping it. Explains why phobias persist. 2. Motivation theories Theory Author Core claim Hierarchy of needs Abraham Maslow Needs climb from physiological → safety → love → esteem → self-actualisation. ERG theory Clayton Alderfer Existence, Relatedness, Growth (Maslow condensed; allows regression). Two-factor (motivation-hygiene) Frederick Herzberg Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivators create satisfaction. Drive-reduction Clark Hull Behaviour reduces physiological drives to restore homeostasis. Arousal theory / Yerkes–Dodson law Yerkes & Dodson Performance peaks at moderate arousal (inverted-U). Self-determination theory Deci & Ryan Intrinsic motivation needs autonomy, competence, relatedness. Expectancy theory Victor Vroom Effort = expectancy × instrumentality × valence. Goal-setting theory Edwin Locke Specific, hard, accepted goals drive higher performance. Need for achievement (nAch) McClelland; Atkinson Achievement/affiliation/power needs; measured via TAT. Flow Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Total absorption when challenge matches skill. Opponent-process theory Richard Solomon Every emotional state triggers an opposing after-reaction (addiction, thrill). Theory X / Theory Y Douglas McGregor Managers either assume workers dislike work and need control (X) or seek responsibility and self-direction (Y). Incentive theory (behaviourist tradition) Behaviour is pulled by external rewards/goals, not just pushed by internal drives. 3. Emotion theories (order of events is the trap) Theory Author Sequence James–Lange James & Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion ("we're afraid because we tremble"). Cannon–Bard Cannon & Bard Stimulus → arousal and emotion simultaneously (thalamic). Schachter–Singer two-factor Schachter & Singer Arousal + cognitive label → emotion. Cognitive appraisal Richard Lazarus Appraisal of the event comes first; cognition precedes emotion. Affective primacy Robert Zajonc Emotion can occur before and without cognition ("preferences need no inferences"). Facial-feedback hypothesis Tomkins; Ekman Facial expressions feed back to intensify/trigger the felt emotion. Basic emotions Paul Ekman Six universal, cross-cultural facial emotions. Wheel of emotions Robert Plutchik Eight primary emotions in opposing pairs, combining into others. The classic swap: James-Lange = body first ; Cannon-Bard = both at once ; Schachter-Singer = arousal + label ; Lazarus = appraisal first ; Zajonc = feeling before thinking . Lazarus vs Zajonc is the famous "primacy of cognition vs affect" debate. 4. The neighbouring sweeps go the other way (concept → person): Theories , Effects . Built 2026-05-24. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How it's asked. "Who proposed X?", "X is associated with whom?", or "Match the theorist to the concept." The distractor is always a same-field contemporary (Freud's circle, the trait theorists, the attachment crew). Learn each person as a bundle so a single concept pulls the whole name up. Jump to: 1. Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian 2. Humanistic & trait 3. Behaviourist & learning 4. Cognitive & developmental 5. Social psychologists 6. Intelligence & testing 7. Statistics & psychometrics 8. Therapy founders 1. Psychoanalytic & neo-Freudian Theorist What they own Sigmund Freud Psychoanalysis; id/ego/superego; psychosexual stages; defence mechanisms; the unconscious; dream interpretation. Carl Jung Analytical psychology; collective unconscious; archetypes; introversion/extraversion; coined the Electra complex; word-association. Alfred Adler Individual psychology; inferiority/superiority complex; striving for superiority; style of life; birth order; social interest. Karen Horney Basic anxiety; moving toward/against/away from people; womb envy (reply to penis envy); neurotic needs. Erik Erikson 8 psychosocial stages; identity crisis; ego psychology. Erich Fromm Escape from Freedom; character orientations; humanistic psychoanalysis. Harry Stack Sullivan Interpersonal theory; the self-system; good-me/bad-me/not-me. Melanie Klein Object relations; play therapy; paranoid-schizoid & depressive positions. Anna Freud Child psychoanalysis; systematised the defence mechanisms. D. W. Winnicott Good-enough mother; transitional object; holding environment; true/false self. Heinz Kohut Self psychology; narcissism; empathic mirroring. Complex ownership: inferiority/superiority = Adler ; womb envy = Horney ; Electra = Jung (named it), Oedipus = Freud. Don't default everything to Freud. 2. Humanistic & trait theorists Theorist What they own Abraham Maslow Hierarchy of needs; self-actualisation; peak experiences; Jonah complex. Carl Rogers Person-centred therapy; self-concept; congruence; unconditional positive regard; fully-functioning person. Gordon Allport Cardinal/central/secondary traits; functional autonomy; idiographic approach; contact hypothesis. Raymond Cattell 16PF; source vs surface traits; fluid vs crystallised intelligence. Hans Eysenck PEN model (Psychoticism, Extraversion, Neuroticism); biological basis of personality. Costa & McCrae Big Five / NEO-PI (OCEAN). Henry Murray Personology; needs & press; the TAT; Icarus complex; nAch roots. George Kelly Personal construct theory; rep grid; "man as scientist." Rollo May / Victor Frankl Existential psychology; May (anxiety/the daimonic); Frankl (logotherapy, meaning). William Sheldon Somatotypes (endo/meso/ectomorph). 3. Behaviourist & learning theorists Theorist What they own Ivan Pavlov Classical conditioning; the salivating dogs. John B. Watson Founded behaviourism; Little Albert; "give me a dozen healthy infants…". B. F. Skinner Operant conditioning; reinforcement schedules; Skinner box; verbal behaviour; radical behaviourism. Edward Thorndike Law of Effect; connectionism; puzzle box; the halo effect. Edward Tolman Latent learning; cognitive maps; purposive behaviourism. Wolfgang Köhler Insight learning (chimps); Gestalt; the bouba/kiki demo. Albert Bandura Social learning; Bobo doll; self-efficacy; reciprocal determinism. Edwin Guthrie Contiguity theory (one-trial learning). Clark Hull Drive-reduction theory; mathematico-deductive behaviourism. Joseph Wolpe Systematic desensitisation; reciprocal inhibition. 4. Cognitive & developmental theorists Theorist What they own Jean Piaget Cognitive-development stages; schemas; assimilation/accommodation; object permanence; conservation. Lev Vygotsky Sociocultural theory; ZPD; scaffolding; private speech. Jerome Bruner Discovery learning; spiral curriculum; enactive/iconic/symbolic; LASS. Lawrence Kohlberg Stages of moral development. Urie Bronfenbrenner Ecological systems; PPCT model. John Bowlby Attachment theory; maternal deprivation; internal working models. Mary Ainsworth Strange Situation; secure/anxious/avoidant attachment. Harry Harlow Rhesus monkeys; contact comfort over food (wire vs cloth mother). Noam Chomsky Universal grammar; LAD; rebutted Skinner; cognitive revolution. Ulric Neisser "Cognitive Psychology" (named the field); ecological memory. Endel Tulving Episodic vs semantic memory; encoding specificity. Baddeley & Hitch Working-memory model. Elizabeth Loftus Misinformation effect; eyewitness memory; false memories. The animal-study set: dogs = Pavlov ; cats/puzzle box = Thorndike ; chimps/insight = Köhler ; monkeys/contact comfort = Harlow ; rats/cognitive maps = Tolman ; Bobo doll = Bandura ; Little Albert = Watson . 5. Social psychologists Theorist What they own Leon Festinger Cognitive dissonance; social comparison; deindividuation roots. Kurt Lewin Father of social psych; field theory; B = f(P,E); action research; group dynamics. Solomon Asch Conformity (line task); impression formation (central traits). Stanley Milgram Obedience to authority; small-world / six degrees. Philip Zimbardo Stanford prison experiment; deindividuation; the Lucifer effect. Muzafer Sherif Realistic conflict; Robbers Cave; autokinetic norm formation. Fritz Heider Attribution theory; balance theory. Lee Ross Coined the fundamental attribution error; false-consensus effect. Tajfel & Turner Social identity theory; minimal group paradigm. Irving Janis Groupthink. Latané & Darley Bystander effect; diffusion of responsibility. Robert Cialdini Six principles of influence.

title: Therapy Components — what belongs to what
text: Therapy Components — what belongs to what Recognition drill for "which of these is a component of ___" items · Built 2026-05-21 Why this page exists. Sihan flagged that the real MET paper asks "which one of these is a component of DBT?" style questions across many therapies. Those are recognition items: they give you 4 things and you pick the one that genuinely belongs. The trap is always a real concept from a different therapy. So for each school below you get two lists: the components that belong and the distractors that don't (and where they actually come from) . Learn both sides and the question becomes free. This is the companion to the full psychotherapy cheatsheet , which covers founders + mechanism. This page is purely "what are the named parts." DBT — Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (Linehan) 4 skill modules: Mindfulness · Distress Tolerance · Emotion Regulation · Interpersonal Effectiveness. Mnemonic: "My Dog Eats Iguanas" (Mindfulness, Distress tolerance, Emotion reg, Interpersonal). 4 modes of treatment: individual therapy · group skills training · phone/between-session coaching · therapist consultation team. NOT a DBT module: "cognitive restructuring" / "cognitive triad" (that's Beck) · "free association" (Freud) · "hexaflex" or "cognitive defusion" (ACT) · "unconditional positive regard" (Rogers). DBT uses acceptance + change ("dialectics") and is built for BPD with chronic suicidality . ACT — Acceptance & Commitment Therapy (Hayes) Hexaflex, 6 processes: Acceptance · Cognitive Defusion · Self-as-Context · Present-Moment Contact · Values · Committed Action. Goal = psychological flexibility (not symptom reduction). NOT ACT: the 4 DBT modules · "ABC model" (Ellis) · "miracle question" (SFBT). If you see "hexaflex," "defusion," "values," or "I'm having the thought that…" it is ACT. CBT — Beck's Cognitive Therapy Components: cognitive triad (negative view of self / world / future) · schemas → automatic thoughts · cognitive distortions (all-or-nothing, overgeneralisation, catastrophising, etc.). Techniques: Socratic questioning (guided discovery) · thought records · downward arrow · behavioural experiments · activity scheduling. NOT Beck: "ABC model / irrational beliefs / dispute" → that's Ellis (REBT) . "Reciprocal inhibition" → Wolpe. The cognitive triad is Beck; the ABC is Ellis. Examiners swap these constantly. REBT — Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (Ellis) ABCDE model: A ctivating event → B elief (rational/irrational) → C onsequence → D ispute → E ffect (new). Core: three irrational demands ("I must do well; others must treat me well; the world must be fair"), aka "musturbation." NOT REBT: "cognitive triad," "automatic thoughts," "Socratic questioning" → Beck. Ellis is more directly confrontational ; Beck uses gentle guided discovery. Person-Centred Therapy (Rogers) 3 core conditions (necessary & sufficient): Empathy · Unconditional Positive Regard (UPR) · Congruence (genuineness). Mnemonic: "EUC" / "the 3 C's if you count empathic-understanding, unconditional-regard, congruence." NOT Rogers: "interpretation," "transference" (Freud) · "empty chair" (Gestalt) · "directive advice" (Rogers is non-directive ). Driver = the client's actualising tendency. Motivational Interviewing (Miller & Rollnick) Spirit — PACE: P artnership · A cceptance · C ompassion · E vocation. 4 processes: Engaging → Focusing → Evoking → Planning. Core skills — OARS: O pen questions · A ffirmations · R eflections · S ummaries. Change talk — DARN-CAT: Desire, Ability, Reason, Need → Commitment, Activation, Taking steps. NOT MI: "confrontation / arguing the client out of it" (the opposite of MI) · "OARS" is MI, not a family-therapy term. Used most for ambivalence in substance use. IPT — Interpersonal Therapy (Klerman & Weissman) 4 problem areas (pick one focus): Grief · Role disputes · Role transitions · Interpersonal deficits. Time-limited (12–16 sessions), originally for depression. NOT IPT: "transference" (it deliberately stays in the here-and-now of relationships, not the past) · "cognitive distortions" (Beck). If you see "role dispute / role transition" it's IPT. Group Therapy — Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors The 11: Instillation of hope · Universality · Imparting information · Altruism · Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group · Development of socialising techniques · Imitative behaviour · Interpersonal learning (the engine) · Group cohesiveness (group analogue of the alliance) · Catharsis · Existential factors. NOT a Yalom factor: "transference interpretation," "free association," "the miracle question." Tag words: social microcosm + here-and-now + interpersonal learning → Yalom. Gestalt Therapy (Perls) Components/techniques: empty chair · top-dog / underdog dialogue · here-and-now awareness · figure-ground · exaggeration · "I" statements · integration of polarities. NOT Gestalt: "free association / dream interpretation" (Freud) · "core conditions" (Rogers). Goal = integrate disowned parts into wholeness. Psychoanalysis / Psychodynamic (Freud) Components/techniques: free association (the fundamental rule) · interpretation of resistance and transference · dream analysis (manifest vs latent) · working through. NOT psychoanalysis: "behavioural experiment," "thought record" (CBT) · "miracle question" (SFBT). Working through = repeated re-encounter with a conflict until integrated, NOT a single interpretation or free association — classic NIMHANS trap. Reality / Choice Therapy (Glasser) WDEP framework: W ants · D oing · E valuation · P lanning. Present-focused, responsibility, "total behaviour." NOT Glasser: "WDEP" is uniquely his — don't confuse with MI's "PACE/OARS" or DBT's modules. Mindfulness-based programmes MBCT (Segal, Williams, Teasdale): 8-week group, MBSR + cognitive therapy. Indication = relapse prevention in recurrent depression (≥3 episodes). MBSR (Kabat-Zinn): 8-week group, body scan + sitting meditation + mindful movement. Stress, chronic pain.
